en: The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, also titled *The Inconceivable Liberation*, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Buddha-land. Chapter One: The Buddha-land.
Thus have I heard: At one time,

the Buddha was staying at the Āmra Grove in Vaiśālī together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus and thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas— all of whom were well-known to the world, had fully accomplished the practices of great wisdom,
were established by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, and upheld the true Dharma as guardians of the city of the Dharma.
Capable of the lion’s roar, their fame resounds throughout the ten directions;
though uninvited by the masses, they act as friends to bring them peace;
they uphold and cause the Three Jewels to flourish so that they shall never be severed.
Having subdued the hosts of Māra and conquered all non-Buddhists, they are entirely pure and forever free from the hindrances and entanglements;
their minds dwell constantly in unimpeded liberation;
and their mindfulness, concentration, dhāraṇī, and eloquence are uninterrupted.
They were fully endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, and power;
they had attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena through the realization of non-apprehension;
and having been able to accord with this, they turned the wheel of non-retrogression.
He skillfully understood the characteristics of phenomena and knew the faculties of sentient beings;
he presided over the great assembly with fearlessness, cultivating his mind through merit and wisdom;
his body was adorned with the primary and secondary marks, his physical form being foremost, yet he had renounced all worldly ornaments.
His fame is lofty and far-reaching, surpassing Mount Sumeru;
his profound faith is steadfast and firm, like a diamond;
the jewel of the Dharma shines universally, raining down ambrosia.
Among all voices and sounds, his is the most subtle and supreme;
he has deeply penetrated dependent origination, severed all false views, and is free from any residual habit regarding the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
He expounds the Dharma with fearlessness like the roar of a lion; that which he preaches is like the crashing of thunder—immeasurable, having transcended all measure.
He gathers the Dharma-treasures of the multitude like a guide across the ocean, thoroughly penetrating the profound and subtle meanings of all phenomena;
he skillfully knows the destinations of sentient beings’ coming and going as well as the movements of their minds;
and he draws near to the peerless, sovereign wisdom of the Buddhas—the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities.
They close the gates to all evil realms, yet manifest their bodies within the five destinies;
acting as great kings of physicians, they skillfully treat all ailments, providing medicine according to the disease so that it may be taken and practiced;
they have fully accomplished immeasurable merits and have purified immeasurable Buddha-lands.
All who see or hear them receive benefit, and whatever they do is never in vain;
they are fully endowed with all such merits—namely:
the Bodhisattva Equal Contemplation, the Bodhisattva Unequal Contemplation, the Bodhisattva Equal-and-Unequal Contemplation, and the Bodhisattva Fixed Self...
The Bodhisattva King, the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Dharma, the Bodhisattva Dharmalakṣaṇa, the Bodhisattva Prabhālakṣaṇa, the Bodhisattva Prabhāvyūha,
the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha, the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa, the Bodhisattva Pratibhānakūṭa, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi,
the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāpāṇi, the Bodhisattva Nityotkṣiptahasta, and the Bodhisattva Nitya...
The Bodhisattva Adhastāt, the Bodhisattva Nityotsāha, the Bodhisattva Pramuditendriya, the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana,
the Bodhisattva Svaravighuṣṭa, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, the Bodhisattva Ratnolkādhara, the Bodhisattva Ratnavīra, the Bodhisattva Ratnapaśya,
the Bodhisattva Indrajāla, the Bodhisattva Jvālājāla, and the Bodhisattva Nirnimittadarśin.
The Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva Jñānasaṃcaya, the Bodhisattva Ratnajaya, the Bodhisattva Devendra, the Bodhisattva Mārapramardin,
the Bodhisattva Vidyudguṇa, the Bodhisattva Vaśavartin, the Bodhisattva Guṇalakṣaṇavyūha,
the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda, the Bodhisattva Meghasvara, the Bodhisattva Parvata-saṃghaṭṭanaruta, and the Bodhisattva Gandha...
The Bodhisattva Gaja, the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin, the Bodhisattva Nityodyukta, the Bodhisattva Anikṣiptadhura,
the Bodhisattva Sujāta, the Bodhisattva Avataṃsaka, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
the Bodhisattva Brahmajāla, the Bodhisattva Ratnadaṇḍa, the Bodhisattva Aparājita, and the Bodhisattva Vyūha.
The Bodhisattva Earth, the Bodhisattva Golden Topknot, the Bodhisattva Pearl Topknot, the Bodhisattva Maitreya,
the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, and others such as these, numbering thirty-two thousand people.
Furthermore, ten thousand Brahma Kings, such as Śikhin and others, came from other four-continent worlds to the place where the Buddha was to listen to the Dharma;
additionally, twelve thousand Śakras also came from other four-continent worlds and sat in the assembly.
Together with other deities of great power—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth—they all came to the assembly and sat down.
The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās all came together and sat in assembly.

At that time, the Buddha was surrounded by a respectful retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of beings as he preached the Dharma for them; like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, rising above the great ocean, he sat upon a lion throne adorned with various jewels, outshining the entire gathered multitude.

At that time, there was a son of an elder in the city of Vaiśālī named Ratnākara, who, together with five hundred sons of elders, each holding a parasol made of the seven precious gems, came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves at his feet and, each with their own parasol, collectively made offerings to the Buddha.

By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, all those precious canopies were merged into a single canopy that completely covered the trichiliocosm; moreover, the vast and extensive features of this world were all manifested within it.

Furthermore, all the Sumeru Mountains, Snowy Mountains, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, Fragrant Mountain, Jewel Mountain, Gold Mountain, Black Mountains, Iron Ring Mountains, and Great Iron Ring Mountains of this trichiliocosm, as well as the great oceans, rivers, streams, springs, and sources, along with the sun, moon, and stars, the palaces of the devas, the palaces of the nāgas, and the palaces of the various honored deities, were all manifested within the precious canopy.
Moreover, the Buddhas of the ten directions and their preaching of the Dharma were likewise manifested within the precious canopy.
At that time, the entire great assembly, beholding the Buddha’s supernatural power, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence!
With palms joined, they prostrated before the Buddha, gazing up at his venerable countenance without averting their eyes for even a moment.
Thereupon, the elder’s son Ratnākara, before the Buddha, spoke in verse:
“Your eyes are pure, long, and wide like blue lotuses; Your mind is pure, having already transcended all meditative concentrations.
Having long accumulated pure karma beyond measure, You lead the multitudes through tranquility; therefore, I bow my head in homage.”
Having seen the Great Sage manifest his spiritual transformations, appearing universally throughout the infinite lands of the ten directions,
and hearing all the Buddhas therein expounding the Dharma, everyone beheld and heard it all.
The Dharma-King’s power of Dharma transcends all living beings; He constantly bestows the wealth of Dharma upon all.
He is able to skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena, And remains unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Having attained mastery over all phenomena, I therefore prostrate to this Dharma-King.
I teach that phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent; All things arise through causes and conditions.
There is no self, no creator, and no experiencer, Yet the karma of good and evil never perishes.
At first, beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued Māra by his power; Having attained the extinction of ambrosia, he perfected the path of awakening.
Already free from mind and thought, and without further mental activity, He completely crushed and subjugated all the non-Buddhists.
He turned the Wheel of Dharma thrice throughout the great universe; that wheel is fundamentally and eternally pure.
That devas and humans have attained the Way serves as its witness; thus the Three Jewels appeared in the world.
With this wondrous Dharma he delivers all living beings; once received, they do not regress and remain eternally tranquil.
The Great Physician King who crosses over old age, sickness, and death—homage should be paid to him, whose Dharma-ocean and virtues are boundless.
Unmoved by praise or blame, like Mount Sumeru; regarding the good and the bad with equal compassion;
his mental conduct is as impartial as space—who, upon hearing of this Human Jewel, would not receive him with reverence?
Now I offer this humble canopy to the World-Honored One;
within it appear my three-thousandfold world system, the palaces where devas, nāgas, and spirits dwell, as well as those of the gandharvas and yakṣas.
All that exists in the world is clearly seen; the One of Ten Powers manifests these transformations out of compassion.
Beholding this rarity, the multitudes all praise the Buddha; now I prostrate before the Honored One of the Three Realms.
The Great Sage, Dharma King, to whom all turn in homage; Those with pure hearts who contemplate the Buddha find no lack of joy.
Each beholds the World-Honored One standing before them; This is the sovereign power of his uncommon dharma.
The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, Yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind.
All believe that the World-Honored One speaks in their own language; this is a spiritual power, an uncommon dharma.
When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each understand according to their own capacity;
they all receive and practice it, obtaining its benefits—this is a spiritual power, an uncommon dharma.
When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, some feel fear, some rejoice, some develop weary detachment, and some sever their doubts; this is the unique power of his spiritual authority.
I prostrate to the One of Ten Powers and Great Diligence; I prostrate to the One who has attained fearlessness;
I prostrate to the One who dwells in the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*); I prostrate to all the Great Teachers;
I prostrate to the One who can sever all fetters and bonds; I prostrate to the One who has already reached the further shore.
I prostrate to the one who can deliver all worlds; I prostrate to the one who has forever left the path of birth and death.
You fully know the signs of the coming and going of sentient beings;
Skillfully attaining liberation through all dharmas, You are unattached to the world like a lotus flower, Constantly and skillfully entering the practice of emptiness and stillness.
"Having attained unimpeded mastery over the characteristics of all phenomena, I prostrate to you who, like space, have no dependence.
At that time, after the elder’s son Ratnākara had spoken this verse, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

These five hundred sons of elders have all already resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They wish to hear how one attains the purity of a Buddha-land; we only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the practices for purifying the lands of bodhisattvas!
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Ratnākara!”
You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the practice of the pure land.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall explain it for you.
Thereupon, Ratnākara and the five hundred sons of elders received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: "Ratnākara!
The various classes of sentient beings constitute the buddha-field of a bodhisattva. Why is this so?

A bodhisattva takes up a buddha-field according to the sentient beings he transforms; he takes up a buddha-field according to the sentient beings he disciplines; he takes up a buddha-field according to the realm through which sentient beings should enter the wisdom of a Buddha; and he takes up a buddha-field according to the realm through which sentient beings should give rise to the faculties of a bodhisattva.
Why is this? It is because when Bodhisattvas take up a pure land, it is entirely for the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings.
It is like a person who wishes to construct a palace upon an empty plot of ground; they may do so as they please without hindrance.
If one attempts this in empty space, it can never be accomplished!
It is the same for a bodhisattva: for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, they vow to take up a Buddha-land; to vow to take up a Buddha-land is not to act within emptiness.
“Ratnakūṭa, you should know this:
a straightforward mind is the pure land of a bodhisattva— when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who are free from deceit will come to be born in that land.”
The profound mind is the bodhisattva’s pure land—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings endowed with perfected merit will come to be born in that land;
the bodhicitta is the bodhisattva’s pure land—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings of the Mahāyāna will come to be born in that land;
giving is the bodhisattva’s pure land—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings capable of total renunciation will come to be born in that land.

Observing the precepts is the pure land of a bodhisattva—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who have fulfilled their vows by practicing the ten paths of wholesome action will come to be born in that land;
patience is the pure land of a bodhisattva—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings adorned with the thirty-two marks will come to be born in that land;
diligence is the pure land of a bodhisattva—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who have diligently cultivated all merits will come to be born in that land.
Meditative concentration is the pure land of a bodhisattva—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings whose minds are collected and undisturbed come to be born in that land;
wisdom is the pure land of a bodhisattva—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who possess right concentration come to be born in that land;

the four immeasurable minds are the pure land of a bodhisattva—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who have perfected loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity come to be born in that land.

The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are the pure land of a bodhisattva—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who have been gathered through liberation come to be born in his land;

skillful means (*upāya*) is the pure land of a bodhisattva—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who possess unimpeded skillful means regarding all dharmas come to be born in his land;

the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) are the pure land of a bodhisattva—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who possess the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and the noble path come to be born in his land.
The mind of dedication is the pure land of a bodhisattva—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, he obtains a land endowed with all perfections;
preaching the removal of the eight difficulties is the pure land of a bodhisattva—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, his land is free from the three evil realms and the eight difficulties;

maintaining one’s own observance of the precepts and not censuring the deficiencies of others is the pure land of a bodhisattva—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, his land is such that even the name of violating prohibitions does not exist.

The ten wholesome paths of action are the pure land of the bodhisattva—when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who have not met with untimely death, who possess great wealth, who practice the Brahma-faring, whose speech is truthful, who always speak with gentle words, whose retinues do not separate from them, who harmonize disputes with goodness, whose words are invariably beneficial, who are without envy, who are without malice, and who possess right view will come to be born in his land.
“In this way, Ratnākara,
as the bodhisattva follows his straightforward mind, he is able to initiate practice;
as he follows his initiation of practice, he attains the profound mind.”
According to the depth of one's mind, the will is subdued;
according to the subduing of the will, one acts as taught;
according to acting as taught, one is able to dedicate [merit].
According to their dedication, there is skillful means;
according to their skillful means, they bring sentient beings to maturity;
according to their maturing of sentient beings, their Buddha-fields become pure.
As the buddha-field is pure, so is the teaching of the Dharma pure;
as the teaching of the Dharma is pure, so is wisdom pure;
as wisdom is pure, so is the mind pure.
As their minds are purified, so all their merits are purified.
Therefore, Ratnākara,
if a bodhisattva wishes to attain a pure land, they should purify their own mind.
“According to the purity of his mind, so too is the Buddha-field pure.
At that time, Śāriputra, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, had this thought:

“If it is the case that when a bodhisattva’s mind is pure, the Buddha-field is pure, then when our World-Honored One was originally a bodhisattva, was his intention not pure, that this Buddha-field is so impure?”
The Buddha, knowing his thought, immediately addressed him, saying:
"What do you think?
Are the sun and moon not pure, yet the blind man does not see them?"
He replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
This is the fault of the blind man, not the fault of the sun and moon."
“Śāriputra! It is because of the transgressions of sentient beings that they do not see the Tathāgata’s buddha-field as adorned and pure; it is not the fault of the Tathāgata. Śāriputra!”
"This land of mine is pure, yet you do not see it.
At that time, the Brahma King Śikhin said to Śāriputra,
"Do not harbor such a thought as to say that this Buddha-field is impure."
"Why is this? I see that the land of Śākyamuni Buddha is pure, just like the palace of the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Śāriputra said:
"I see this land as full of mounds, hills, ravines, pits, thorns, gravel, sand, stones, and various mountains, filled with filth and impurity.
The Brahma King Śikhin said, "Virtuous one,
because your mind has highs and lows and does not rely upon the Buddha’s wisdom, you see this land as impure!"

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva is entirely impartial toward all sentient beings, possesses a profoundly pure mind, and relies upon the wisdom of the Buddha, they are then able to see this buddha-field as pure.

Thereupon, the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe, and immediately this trichiliocosm was adorned with hundreds of thousands of various precious jewels, like the Land of Immeasurable Merit Adorned with Jewels belonging to the Buddha Ratnavyūha. The entire great assembly marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, and each saw themselves sitting upon a precious lotus flower.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
“Do you observe how this buddha-field is adorned and purified?
Śāriputra replied:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
That which was never before seen and never before heard is now fully manifested as the majestic purity of the Buddha-land.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"My Buddha-land is always pure like this; it is only because I wish to deliver those of inferior capacity that I manifest this land of manifold evils and impurity.
It is just as when the various devas eat from a common precious vessel: according to their respective merits, the color of the food appears different."
"In this way, Śāriputra,
if a person’s mind is pure, they will see the adornments of merit of this land.

When the Buddha manifested the purity and splendor of this land, all five hundred sons of elders brought by Ratnākara attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and eighty-four thousand people all resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha withdrew his supernormal power, and this world was restored to its former state.

Thirty-two thousand devas and humans who sought the vehicle of the śrāvakas, realizing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are entirely impermanent, became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Eight thousand bhikṣus, no longer grasping at any phenomena, attained the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

Chapter Two: On Skillful Means (*Upāya-kauśalya*) At that time, in the great city of Vaiśālī, there was an elder named Vimalakīrti. He had already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, deeply planted the roots of goodness, and attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
His eloquence was unimpeded, he sported with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), and he had mastered all dhāraṇīs.
Having attained fearlessness, he subdued Māra and his host of enemies.
They have entered profound Dharma-gates, are skilled in the Perfection of Wisdom, and have mastered expedient means; their great vows are fulfilled.

They clearly understand the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings and can discern the sharpness or dullness of their faculties. Having long practiced the Buddha-way, their minds are already pure and mature, and they are firmly resolved upon the Mahāyāna.
In all that they do, they are able to exercise skillful deliberation.
Abiding in the majestic deportment of a Buddha, his mind was as vast as the ocean; he was praised by all Buddhas and revered by disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and the lords of the world.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, he dwelt in Vaiśālī through skillful means;
possessing immeasurable wealth, he gathered in the poor and destitute.
By maintaining pure precepts, they gather in those who violate the prohibitions;
by tempering their conduct with patience, they gather in those who harbor anger;
and by means of great diligence, they gather in those who are indolent.
With single-minded meditative stillness, he restrained all distracted thoughts;
with resolute wisdom, he restrained all ignorance;
though he was a layman, he upheld the pure disciplinary conduct of a śramaṇa.
Though dwelling in the household life, he is not attached to the triple world;
though appearing to have a wife and children, he constantly cultivates pure conduct;
though having kinsmen and attendants, he always delights in solitude and detachment.
Although he wears precious ornaments, he adorns his body with the marks and signs of excellence;
although he partakes of food and drink, he takes the joy of dhyāna as his true flavor;
and whenever he arrives at places of gambling or games, he immediately uses them to deliver others.
He may undergo the practices of various heterodox paths, yet he does not disparage his correct faith;
though he is learned in worldly classics, he always delights in the Buddha-dharma;
he is respected by all, becoming the foremost among those who receive offerings.
Upholding the True Dharma, they guide both the elderly and the young;
in all their worldly livelihoods, they act with harmony and propriety, yet they do not feel joy even when obtaining secular profit;
they travel through the four crossroads to benefit all sentient beings.
Entering into the administration of government and legal affairs, he protects and delivers all beings;
entering into places of debate and discussion, he guides them with the Mahāyāna;
entering into various schools, he entices and enlightens the ignorant.
He enters brothels to demonstrate the faults of desire;
he enters taverns to establish their resolve;
and when among elders, he is honored as the most venerable, preaching the supreme Dharma for them.
If among householders, he is the most honored among householders, severing their greedy attachments;
if among kṣatriyas, he is the most honored among kṣatriyas, instructing them in patience;
if among brahmins, he is the most honored among brahmins, eliminating their arrogance.
If among ministers, he is the most honored among ministers and instructs them with the True Dharma;
if among princes, he is the most honored among princes and demonstrates loyalty and filial piety;
if among inner officials, he is the most honored among inner officials and transforms the palace women through his governance.
If among the common people, he is the most honored among them, causing them to arouse the power of merit;
if among the Brahmā devas, he is the most honored among them, instructing them with supreme wisdom;
if among Śakra, he is the most honored among them, manifesting the impermanence of all things.
If he was among the World Protectors (*Lokapāla*), he was the most honored among them, protecting all sentient beings;
the Elder Vimalakīrti benefited sentient beings through such immeasurable skillful means as these.
By means of skillful expedients, he manifested himself as being ill.
Because of this illness, kings, ministers, elders, householders, brahmins, and others—including princes and their various retinues—numbering many thousands, all went to inquire after his health.
When he went there, Vimalakīrti used his own physical illness as an occasion to preach the Dharma extensively:
"O worthy ones!
This body is impermanent, lacks strength, lacks power, and lacks solidity; it is a thing that quickly decays and cannot be relied upon!"
It is suffering and affliction, the gathering place of all maladies.
O worthy ones!
Such a body as this is not to be relied upon by those of wisdom.
This body is like a mass of foam, incapable of being grasped or rubbed;
this body is like a bubble, unable to endure for long;
this body is like a mirage, born from craving and thirst.
This body is like a plantain tree, having no solidity within;
this body is like an illusion, arising from perversion;
this body is like a dream, a false perception.
This body is like a shadow, appearing through the conditions of karma;
this body is like an echo, dependent upon various causes and conditions;
this body is like a floating cloud, changing and perishing in an instant.
This body is like lightning, not abiding for even a single thought-moment;
this body has no master, being like the earth;
this body has no self, being like fire.
This body has no life-span, being like the wind;
this body has no person, being like water;
this body is unreal, having the four great elements as its abode.
This body is empty, devoid of self and what belongs to self;
this body is insentient, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles;
this body is inactive, driven by the power of the winds.
This body is impure, filled with filth and evil;
this body is deceptive, for though it is provisionally sustained by bathing, clothing, and food, it inevitably returns to decay and extinction;
this body is a calamity, afflicted by one hundred and one maladies.
This body is like a well beside a mound, oppressed by old age;
this body is without permanence, for it must inevitably die;
this body is like a venomous snake, like a hostile thief, like an empty village—a composite formation of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
"O virtuous ones!
This [body] is to be weary of and loathe; you should instead take delight in the Buddha-body. Why is this so?
The Buddha-body is precisely the Dharma-body!

Born from immeasurable merit and wisdom; born from precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; born from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; born from the various *pāramitās* of giving, ethical discipline, patience, gentleness, diligent exertion, meditative concentration, liberation, samādhi, extensive learning, and wisdom; born from skillful means; born from the six supernormal powers; born from the three types of clear knowledge; born from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; born from tranquility and insight; born from the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; born from the abandonment of all unwholesome dharmas and the accumulation of all wholesome dharmas; born from reality; born from heedfulness.
The body of the Tathāgata is born from such immeasurable, pure dharmas.
"O virtuous ones!
Those who wish to attain the body of a Buddha and sever all the illnesses of sentient beings should resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

In this manner, the elder Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma to those who had come to inquire after his illness as was appropriate for each, causing countless thousands of people to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Chapter Three: The Disciples The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra, Chapter Three: The Disciples At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti thought to himself:
"I lie ill upon my bed; surely the World-Honored One, in his great compassion, will not fail to show me pity?"
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, immediately addressed Śāriputra:
"Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Śāriputra said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go there to inquire about his illness. Why is this? Because—”
I recall that in the past, while I was sitting in meditative seclusion beneath a tree in a forest, Vimalakīrti came to me and said: "O Śāriputra!..."
It is not necessarily sitting cross-legged that constitutes "sitting in repose.
As for sitting in repose: not manifesting body or mind within the three realms is sitting in repose;
not arising from the meditative concentration of cessation while manifesting various dignified behaviors is sitting in repose.
To manifest the affairs of an ordinary person without abandoning the Dharma of the Path—this is the practice of sitting in meditation.
For the mind to dwell neither within nor without—this is the practice of sitting in meditation.
To remain unmoved by various views while practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—this is the practice of sitting in meditation.
"To enter nirvana without severing the afflictions—this is true sitting in meditation.
If one can sit in this manner, it is approved by the Buddha.
At that time, O World-Honored One, I...
—Upon hearing these words, he fell silent and ceased speaking, unable to offer a reply; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
The Buddha said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
“Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.”
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.”
Why is this? I recall that in the past,
when I had entered the great city of Vaiśālī and was teaching the Dharma to the lay devotees in the midst of the lanes and alleys,
Vimalakīrti came to me and said:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
When preaching the Dharma to lay householders, you should not preach as you have just done.
One who preaches the Dharma should preach it in accordance with the Dharma."
The Dharma has no sentient beings, for it is free from the defilement of sentient beings;
the Dharma has no self, for it is free from the defilement of the self;
the Dharma has no life-span, for it is free from birth and death.
Dharmas have no person, for their past and future limits are severed;
dharmas are eternally quiescent, for they extinguish all marks;
dharmas are free from marks, for they have no object of perception.
The Dharma has no names, for it transcends speech;
the Dharma has no discourse, for it is free from applied and sustained thought;
the Dharma has no form or characteristics, for it is like empty space.
Dharmas are without conceptual proliferation, because they are ultimately empty;
dharmas have no sense of "mine," because they are free from the notion of "mine";
dharmas are without discrimination, because they are free from all consciousnesses.
Dharmas have no counterpart, for they do not depend on one another;
dharmas do not belong to causes, for they do not abide in conditions;
dharmas are identical with the dharma-nature, for they enter into all phenomena.
The Dharma conforms to suchness because there is nothing to which it conforms;
the Dharma abides in the limit of reality because it is unmoved by any extremes;
the Dharma is without fluctuation because it does not rely on the six sense objects.
Dharmas have no going or coming, for they never abide;
dharmas accord with emptiness, follow signlessness, and respond to wishlessness;
dharmas are free from the beautiful and the ugly; dharmas have no increase or decrease; dharmas have no arising or ceasing; dharmas have no place of return.
The Dharma transcends the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
the Dharma has no high or low, the Dharma is eternally abiding and immovable, and the Dharma is detached from all modes of contemplation and practice.
"Indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Such is the nature of dharmas; how could they be spoken?
For one who preaches the Dharma, there is neither speaking nor showing."
Those who listen to the Dharma neither hear nor attain anything; they are like illusory beings preaching the Dharma for illusory people. One should establish this intention when preaching the Dharma.

Having understood that the faculties of sentient beings vary between sharp and dull, being skilled in knowledge and vision without any obstruction, praising the Mahāyāna with a heart of great compassion, and mindful of repaying the Buddha’s kindness while ensuring the continuity of the Triple Gem, one should then preach the Dharma.
"When Vimalakīrti preached this Dharma, eight hundred lay devotees resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
I lack such eloquence; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness."
The Buddha said to Mahākāśyapa,
“Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this? Because—”
I recall that in the past, while I was begging for alms in a poor neighborhood, Vimalakīrti came and said to me:
"O Mahākāśyapa! You possess a heart of compassion, yet you do not extend it universally; you abandon the wealthy and seek alms from the poor."
Kāśyapa! Abiding in the dharma of equality, one should practice alms-gathering in due order.

One should practice alms-gathering for the sake of non-eating; one should take morsel-food for the sake of destroying the perception of combination; and one should accept that food for the sake of non-acceptance.

With the perception of an empty village, one enters the village; whatever forms are seen are like those of the blind; whatever sounds are heard are like echoes; whatever scents are smelled are like the wind; whatever flavors are tasted are not discriminated; whatever contacts are experienced are realized through wisdom; and one knows that all phenomena are like illusory appearances, lacking self-nature and lacking other-nature, being fundamentally non-arising and thus now non-extinguishing.
Kāśyapa!

If one can enter the eight liberations without abandoning the eight wrong paths, entering the true Dharma by means of the characteristics of the wrong, and if one gives a single meal to all beings as an offering to all Buddhas and the assembly of worthy sages, only then may one eat.

One who eats in this manner has neither afflictions nor is free from afflictions; they have neither entered a state of meditative concentration nor arisen from it; they abide neither in the world nor in nirvana.
If there is one who gives, there is neither great merit nor small merit; it is neither for benefit nor for harm. This is called entering the Buddha-way correctly, not relying on the Śrāvakas.
Kāśyapa!
"If one eats in this manner, one does not eat the alms of others in vain.

World-Honored One, at that time, having heard these words, I attained what I had never experienced before; I immediately conceived a profound heart of reverence for all bodhisattvas and further thought to myself:
"To possess such a name as 'Householder' and yet to have eloquence and wisdom like this!
Who, upon hearing this, would not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
"Since that time, I have no longer encouraged others in the practices of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
For this reason, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this?
I recall that in the past, when I entered his house to beg for alms, Vimalakīrti took my bowl, filled it with food, and said to me:
"O Subhūti! If one can be equal toward food, then all dharmas are also equal; if all dharmas are equal, then one is also equal toward food.
One who practices alms-gathering in this manner may accept food."
If Subhūti does not sever lust, anger, and delusion, yet is not associated with them;
does not destroy the body, yet conforms to the single mark;
does not extinguish ignorance and craving, yet gives rise to clarity and liberation;
One attains liberation through the characteristics of the five heinous crimes, yet is neither liberated nor bound;
one does not perceive the Four Noble Truths, yet it is not that one does not perceive the truths;
one does not attain the fruits [of the path], yet it is not that one does not attain the fruits.
He is not an ordinary person, yet he is not apart from the dharmas of ordinary persons;
he is not a noble one, yet he is not a non-noble one.
Although he has accomplished all dharmas, he is detached from the marks of all dharmas; only then may you accept this food.

Subhūti, if you do not see the Buddha and do not hear the Dharma, and if those six non-Buddhist teachers—Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarin Gośālīputra, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra—were your teachers; if you had left the household life because of them, and if you were to fall wherever those teachers fell, only then may you accept this food.
If Subhūti were to enter into various false views, he would not reach the other shore;
if he were to dwell in the eight difficult conditions, he would not obtain freedom from difficulty;
if he were identical with afflictions, he would be separated from the dharma of purity.
If you were to attain the Samādhi of Non-contention, all sentient beings would likewise attain this samādhi.

Those who give to you would not be called fields of merit; those who make offerings to you would fall into the three evil realms. You would be acting in concert with the various Māras, serving as their companions in toil. You would be no different from the Māras and the afflictions themselves. You would harbor enmity toward all sentient beings, slander the Buddhas, and destroy the Dharma. You would not be counted among the assembly and would ultimately never attain nirvana.
"If you can do so, only then may you take this food.
At that time, World-Honored One,
having heard these words, I was utterly bewildered and did not know what they meant.
Not knowing how to answer,
he set down his bowl and was about to leave the house when Vimalakīrti said:
"O Subhūti! Take the bowl; do not be afraid.
What do you think?"
"If a person created as a transformation by the Tathāgata were to be questioned on this matter,
would they feel any fear? I replied, "No!"
Vimalakīrti said:
"All dharmas are like illusions and transformations; you should not feel any fear regarding them now. Why is this?'"
All verbal expressions do not depart from these characteristics; yet for the wise, because they do not cling to words, they have nothing to fear.
Why is this? The nature of words is detached; where there are no words, that is liberation.
"The characteristic of liberation is, in fact, all phenomena.
When Vimalakīrti spoke this Dharma, two hundred devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
The Buddha said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
“Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this? Because—”
I recall that in the past, while I was in a great forest preaching the Dharma to newly ordained bhikṣus beneath a tree,
Vimalakīrti came and said to me: "O Pūrṇa!..."
First you should enter meditative concentration and observe this person’s mind before preaching the Dharma.
Do not place foul food in a precious vessel; you should know the thoughts in this bhikṣu’s mind, and do not treat lapis lazuli as if it were common crystal.
"You do not know the fundamental dispositions of sentient beings; do not initiate them with the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle.
They have no sores themselves, so do not wound them.
Those who wish to travel the Great Road, do not show them the narrow path."
Do not attempt to contain the great ocean within the footprint of an ox;
do not equate the light of the sun with that of a firefly. Pūrṇa!
This bhikṣu has long since resolved his mind upon the Mahāyāna, yet he has temporarily forgotten this intention; how can he be instructed by means of the Hīnayāna?
I observe that the wisdom of the Hīnayāna is feeble and shallow, like that of a blind person, unable to discern the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings.
Then Vimalakīrti immediately entered into samādhi, causing these bhikṣus to recognize their own past lives:
that they had planted the roots of various virtues under five hundred buddhas and dedicated them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Instantly, their minds were suddenly enlightened as they recovered their original nature; thereupon, the bhikṣus bowed their heads in prostration at the feet of Vimalakīrti.
Then Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma for them, and they became irreversible from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"I recall that as a śrāvaka, I do not examine the faculties of others before preaching the Dharma; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Mahākātyāyana, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire about his illness."
Kātyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.”

Why is this? I recall that in the past, when the Buddha had briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the bhikṣus, I subsequently elaborated upon their meaning—namely, the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of suffering, the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of non-self, and the meaning of cessation.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me:
"O Kātyāyana! Do not explain the Dharma of the true mark with a mind characterized by arising and ceasing."
Kātyāyana! That all dharmas are ultimately neither born nor extinguished is the meaning of impermanence;
that one penetrates the five aggregates of clinging as empty and without arising is the meaning of suffering.
That all phenomena are ultimately non-existent is the meaning of emptiness;
that self and non-self are non-dual is the meaning of non-self;
that phenomena were originally not ignited and thus now do not extinguish is the meaning of quiescent extinction.
When this Dharma was being taught, the minds of those bhikṣus were liberated.
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Aniruddha:
"Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire about his illness.
Aniruddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this?

I recall that once, while I was walking in meditation at a certain place, a Brahmā King named Śuddhāvāsa arrived together with ten thousand Brahmās, emitting pure light. He came to where I was, prostrated himself in salutation, and asked me:
"How far, Ānanda, can you see with your divine eye?
I then replied: "Venerable sir!
"I see this Sahā world-system of Śākyamuni Buddha’s land as clearly as one would look at an *āmala* fruit in the palm of one's hand.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "O Aniruddha!..."
Is that which is seen by the divine eye characterized by activity (*sābhisaṃskāra*) or characterized by non-activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*)?
If it were characterized by activity, it would be equal to the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of the non-Buddhists;
if it were characterized by non-activity, it would be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and thus there should be no seeing.
"World-Honored One!
At that time, I remained silent.
When those Brahmās heard these words, they experienced what they had never before encountered; they immediately paid homage and asked: "
"Who in the world possesses the true divine eye?
Vimalakīrti replied, "There is."
"The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has attained the true divine eye; he constantly abides in samādhi and perceives all buddha-lands without perceiving them as dualistic forms.

Thereupon, the Brahma King Śuddhāvāsa and his retinue of five hundred Brahmās all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having prostrated at the feet of Vimalakīrti, they suddenly vanished.
"Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
The Buddha said to Upāli,
"Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness."
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I am not capable of going to him to inquire about his illness.”
Why is this? I recall that in the past, there were two bhikṣus who had committed violations of the disciplinary rules. Feeling ashamed, they did not dare to ask the Buddha, but came to me and said:
"Venerable Upāli!..."

"We have violated the precepts and truly feel ashamed; we did not dare to question the Buddha, yet we pray that you will resolve our doubts and regrets so that we may be freed from this transgression.
I then explained the Dharma for them according to the law.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me:
"O Upāli! Do not further increase the transgressions of these two bhikṣus!"
You should immediately eliminate them and not disturb your mind. Why is this?

The nature of those offenses is neither within, nor without, nor in between. As the Buddha has said: "Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure."
The mind is neither within, nor without, nor in between; as it is with the mind, so it is with sinful defilements, and so it is with all phenomena—they do not transcend suchness.
"Upāli! When one attains liberation through the characteristic of the mind, is there any defilement present? I replied:
"No," said Vimalakīrti,
"the nature of the minds of all sentient beings is likewise free from defilement."
"Indeed, Upāli! Conceptual proliferation is defilement;
the absence of conceptual proliferation is purity.
Inversion is defilement; the absence of inversion is purity."
To grasp at a self is defilement; not to grasp at a self is purity. Upāli!
All phenomena arise and perish without abiding; they are like illusions and like lightning. Phenomena do not wait for one another, not even for a single thought-moment.
All phenomena are false perceptions, like a dream, like a mirage, like the moon reflected in water, like an image in a mirror; they arise from deluded thought.
He who knows this is said to uphold the discipline;
he who knows this is said to have a thorough understanding.
Thereupon, the two bhikṣus said:
"How supreme is this wisdom!
It is beyond the reach of Upāli; though he is the foremost in upholding the Vinaya, he cannot explain it."
I immediately replied:
"Aside from the Tathāgata himself, there has never been a śrāvaka or bodhisattva capable of restraining his eloquence in joyful exposition; such is the brilliance and penetration of his wisdom!"
At that time, the doubts and regrets of the two bhikṣus were immediately dispelled, and they resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, making this vow:
"May all sentient beings attain such eloquence as this."
"Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Rāhula,
"Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire about his illness."
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.”
Why is this? I recall that in the past, the sons of the elders of Vaiśālī came to where I was, prostrated themselves in salutation, and asked me: "O Rāhula!..."
"You are a son of the Buddha; having renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch, you have left the household life to pursue the Way.
What are the benefits of such renunciation?
I then explained to him, in accordance with the Dharma, the merits and benefits of leaving the household life.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me:
"O Rāhula! You should not speak of the benefits and merits of leaving the household life."
Why is this so? That which is without benefit and without merit is what constitutes "leaving home" (renunciation);
as for conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma), it can be said that they possess both benefit and merit.
Now, one who has gone forth practices the unconditioned dharma; within the unconditioned dharma, there is neither benefit nor merit.
Rāhula! One who has gone forth is without "that" or "this," nor is there anything between them.
Free from the sixty-two views, they abide in nirvana;
this is what the wise receive and where the sages practice.
They subdue all Māras, deliver beings from the five realms of existence, purify the five eyes, attain the five powers, and establish the five faculties.
Not causing affliction to others, one is free from all manner of evil;
one subdues all heterodox paths and transcends provisional names;
emerging from the mire, one is without attachment.
Without the notion of "mine" and without grasping;
without agitation, harboring joy within;
protecting the minds of others, following meditative concentration, and free from all faults.
"If one can act in this way, that is true renunciation.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti said to the sons of the elders, "Among you,
it is fitting that you all renounce the world together within the True Dharma."
"Why is this? Because it is difficult to encounter a Buddha in the world!
The sons of the elders said:
"Householder!
I have heard the Buddha say that one may not go forth into homelessness without the permission of one's parents.
Vimalakīrti said:
"Indeed! If you all simply give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, that itself is renunciation and that itself is full ordination.
At that time, the thirty-two sons of the elders all gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this? Because—”
I recall that in the past, when the World-Honored One was slightly indisposed and required cow’s milk, I immediately took my alms bowl and went to stand at the gate of a great brāhmaṇa’s house.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me:
"Venerable Ānanda,
why are you standing here at dawn holding your alms bowl?"
I said: "Householder!
The World-Honored One has a slight ailment and requires cow's milk; therefore, I have come here."
Vimalakīrti said: "Stop, stop, Ānanda!"
Do not speak such words!
The body of the Tathāgata is of vajra substance; all evils have been severed, and all virtues are universally assembled. How could he have any illness?
"What cause for vexation could there be?
Go in silence, Ānanda!"
Do not slander the Tathāgata; do not let others hear such coarse words;
do not allow the devas of great majesty and power, nor the bodhisattvas who have come from the pure lands of other directions, to hear these words.
Ānanda! If even a Wheel-Turning Sage King, by virtue of his meager merit, remains free from illness, how much more so the Tathāgata, who has gathered immeasurable merit and is universally supreme?
Go, Ānanda! Do not cause us to suffer this disgrace.
If the heterodox teachers and brahmins hear these words, they will think thus:
"What is meant by being a teacher?
One who cannot save himself from his own illness—how can he save others from their illnesses?
You, O Benevolent One, should depart in secret and with haste; do not let anyone hear of this."
"You should know, Ānanda,
that the bodies of all Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body, not a body of thought or desire.
The Buddha is the World-Honored One, transcending the three realms."
The Buddha’s body is without outflows, for all outflows have been exhausted;
the Buddha’s body is unconditioned, and does not fall within the realm of numerical reckoning.
For such a body as this, how could there be any illness?
"How could there be any cause for distress?
At that time, World-Honored One, I was truly filled with shame and remorse, thinking: "Could it be that I am near the Buddha yet have misunderstood his words?"
Immediately, a voice was heard from the air, saying:
"Ānanda! It is as the householder has said."
It is only because the Buddha has appeared in this world of five turbidities that he manifests these practices to deliver and liberate sentient beings. Go, Ānanda!
Take the milk without feeling ashamed.
"World-Honored One!
Such is the wisdom and eloquence of Vimalakīrti!
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness."

In this manner, each of the five hundred great disciples spoke to the Buddha regarding their own past causes and conditions, recounting the words spoken by Vimalakīrti; they all declared that they were unable to go to him to inquire after his illness.
Chapter Four: The Bodhisattvas. In the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Chapter Four, "The Bodhisattvas," the Buddha then addressed the bodhisattva Maitreya:
"Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness."
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.”
Why is this? I recall that in the past,
when I was preaching the practice of the stage of non-retrogression for the King of Tuṣita Heaven and his retinue,
Vimalakīrti came and said to me:
“Maitreya! The World-Honored One has bestowed upon you the prediction that in one more birth you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
By means of which birth do you receive this prediction?”
Is it the past?
Is it the future?
Or is it the present?
If it is birth in the past, that past birth has already ceased;
if it is birth in the future, that future birth has not yet arrived;
if it is birth in the present, that present birth has no abiding.
As the Buddha has said:
"Bhikṣus! At this very moment, you are also being born, aging, and ceasing."

"If one receives a prediction of enlightenment through non-arising, then non-arising is itself the state of true reality (bhūtakoti). Within this state of true reality, there is neither receiving a prediction nor attaining unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). How then can Maitreya receive the prediction of being born only once more?"
Is one granted the prediction of enlightenment by virtue of the arising of suchness?
Or is one granted the prediction by virtue of the cessation of suchness?
If one were granted the prediction by virtue of the arising of suchness, suchness would have no arising.
If one were to receive a prediction based on the extinction of suchness, there would be no extinction of suchness.
All sentient beings are suchness; all dharmas are also suchness; all noble sages are also suchness; and even Maitreya is likewise suchness.
If Maitreya receives a prediction of enlightenment, then all sentient beings should also receive a prediction. Why is this?
Because Suchness is neither dual nor differentiated; if Maitreya attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then all sentient beings should likewise attain it.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings are themselves the mark of bodhi.
If Maitreya were to attain parinirvāṇa, then all sentient beings would likewise attain parinirvāṇa.
Why is this so? Because all Buddhas know that all sentient beings are ultimately quiescent, possessing the very nature of nirvana, and do not undergo further extinction.
Therefore, Maitreya!
Do not use this Dharma to entice these sons of the gods; in reality, there is no one who has set their mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor is there anyone who falls back from it.
Maitreya!
I shall cause these sons of the gods to abandon their conceptual views regarding bodhi. Why is this?
Because bodhi cannot be attained by means of the body, nor can it be attained by means of the mind.
Quiescence is bodhi, because it extinguishes all marks;
non-contemplation is bodhi, because it is free from all conditions;
non-action is bodhi, because it is devoid of recollection and thought.
Enlightenment is cessation, because it relinquishes all views;
enlightenment is detachment, because it is free from all delusive thoughts;
enlightenment is obstruction, because it obstructs all worldly vows.
This awakening does not enter, because it is free from craving and attachment;
this awakening accords with reality, because it accords with suchness;
this awakening abides, because it abides in the dharma-nature.
Awakening is reaching the limit of reality, for it reaches the ultimate limit;
awakening is non-duality, for it is free from the mind and its objects;
awakening is equality, for it is equal to empty space.
Unconditioned is bodhi, because it is without arising, abiding, or ceasing;
knowledge is bodhi, because it fully understands the mental activities of sentient beings;
non-union is bodhi, because there is no union with the sense bases.
Enlightenment is non-conforming, because it is free from the habitual tendencies of afflictions;
enlightenment is placeless, because it has no form or color;
enlightenment is a provisional name, because names are empty.
Awakening is like a magical transformation, for it is free from grasping and rejecting;
awakening is without distraction, for it is eternally quiescent;
awakening is sublime tranquility, for its nature is pure.
Enlightenment is without grasping, because it is free from objective conditions;
enlightenment is without differentiation, because all phenomena are equal;
enlightenment is beyond comparison, because there is nothing with which it can be likened.
“Subtle is bodhi, for all dharmas are difficult to know.
World-Honored One,
when Vimalakīrti spoke this Dharma, two hundred devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
"Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
The Buddha said to the youth Prabhāvyūha,
"Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness."
Prabhāvyūha addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.”
Why is this? I recall that in the past, when I was leaving the great city of Vaiśālī, Vimalakīrti was entering the city. I immediately paid him homage and asked:
"Householder, from where have you come?"
He replied to me, saying:
"I have come from the place of enlightenment. I asked:
"What is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)?
He replied:
"The straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment, because it is free from falsehood."
The practice of giving is the site of enlightenment, for it accomplishes all tasks;
the profound resolve is the site of enlightenment, for it increases merit and virtue;
the bodhicitta is the site of enlightenment, for it is free from error.
Generosity is the site of enlightenment, because it is free from expectation of reward;
ethical discipline is the site of enlightenment, because it fulfills one's vows;
patience is the site of enlightenment, because the mind is unimpeded toward all sentient beings.
Diligence is the site of awakening, because it is free from indolence and regression;
meditative concentration is the site of awakening, because the mind is harmonized and supple;
wisdom is the site of awakening, because one directly perceives all phenomena.
Loving-kindness is the site of enlightenment, because it treats all sentient beings with equality;
compassion is the site of enlightenment, because it endures weariness and suffering;
joy is the site of enlightenment, because it delights in the Dharma.
Equanimity is the site of enlightenment, for it severs both hatred and attachment;
supernormal powers are the site of enlightenment, for they bring the six penetrations to fulfillment;
liberation is the site of enlightenment, for it enables one to turn away from and relinquish all things.
Skillful means are the site of enlightenment, for they transform and guide sentient beings;
the four methods of attraction are the site of enlightenment, for they gather in sentient beings;
extensive learning is the site of enlightenment, for one acts in accordance with what has been heard.
Subduing the mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because it correctly contemplates all phenomena;
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the site of enlightenment, because they relinquish conditioned phenomena;
the truths are the site of enlightenment, because they do not deceive the world.
Dependent origination is the site of awakening, because from ignorance through to old age and death, all are inexhaustible;
the various afflictions are the site of awakening, because they are known as they truly are;
sentient beings are the site of awakening, because they are known to be without self.
All dharmas are the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because one knows all dharmas to be empty;
subduing Māra is the site of enlightenment, because one is unshakable;
the three realms are the site of enlightenment, because there is no place of destination.
The lion’s roar is the site of enlightenment, because it is free from fear;
the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities are the site of enlightenment, because they are free from all faults;
the three types of supernormal knowledge are the site of enlightenment, because they are free from all remaining obstructions.
"To know all dharmas in a single thought is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), for it is the accomplishment of all-knowledge.
Thus, son of good family,

if a bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings in accordance with the various pāramitās, whatever they do— whether lifting a foot or setting it down— one should know that it all proceeds from the site of enlightenment and abides within the Buddha-dharma."
When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred devas and humans all resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Lokadhara,
"Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Lokadhara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this? Because—”

I recall that in the past, while I was dwelling in a quiet chamber, Māra Pāpīyān approached me accompanied by twelve thousand celestial maidens; he appeared in the guise of Śakra, playing music and singing songs with lutes.
Together with his retinue, he bowed his head at my feet, joined his palms in reverence, and stood to one side.
I thought to myself that this was Śakra, and I spoke to him, saying:
"Welcome, Kauśika!"
Although one may rightfully possess merit, one should not indulge in self-indulgence.
One should contemplate the impermanence of the five desires in order to seek the root of goodness, and cultivate the steadfast Dharma regarding body, life, and wealth.
He then said to me: "O Noble One!
Accept these twelve thousand celestial maidens to serve as your attendants for sweeping and cleaning."
I said: "Kauśika!
Do not offer these improper things to me, a śramaṇa son of the Śākyas; this is not suitable for me."
Before he had finished speaking, Vimalakīrti arrived and said to me, "This is not Śakra;
it is Māra who has come to harass and obstruct you!"
He then said to Māra, "Give these women to me; they are as one such as I ought to receive.
Māra was immediately struck with fear and thought:
"Could it be that Vimalakīrti intends to trouble me?
Thinking thus, he wished to vanish from sight and depart, but he could not vanish;
even by exhausting his supernatural powers, he was still unable to leave.
Immediately, a voice was heard from the air, saying:
"Pāpīyān! Give him your daughters, and only then may you depart."
Out of fear, Māra reluctantly handed them over.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to the maidens, "Māra has given you all to me;
now you must all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
He then preached the Dharma to them according to their needs, causing them to resolve upon the path.
He further said:
"Now that you have resolved upon the path, there is the joy of the Dharma with which you may find delight; you should no longer take pleasure in the five sensual desires."
The goddess then asked,
"What is meant by the joy of the Dharma?
He replied:
"Delighting in constant faith in the Buddha; delighting in the desire to hear the Dharma; delighting in making offerings to the Saṃgha; delighting in detachment from the five desires;
delighting in viewing the five aggregates as enemies and robbers; delighting in viewing the four great elements as venomous snakes; delighting in viewing the internal sense bases as an empty village;
delighting in following and protecting the resolve for enlightenment; delighting in benefiting sentient beings; and delighting in reverently supporting one's teacher."

They delight in extensively practicing giving; they delight in firmly upholding the precepts; they delight in patience, gentleness, and flexibility; they delight in diligently accumulating roots of goodness; they delight in meditative concentration without distraction; they delight in stainless, luminous wisdom;

they delight in expanding the bodhicitta; they delight in subduing all māras; they delight in severing all afflictions; they delight in purifying buddha-fields; and they delight in perfecting the primary and secondary marks by cultivating all meritorious virtues; they delight in adorning the site of enlightenment.
They delight in hearing the profound Dharma and do not fear it;
they delight in the three gates of liberation and do not delight in what is untimely;
they delight in associating with fellow practitioners, and even among those who are not fellow practitioners, their minds are free from anger and obstruction.
Delighting in protecting against evil associates, delighting in drawing near to virtuous friends;
delighting in a joyful and pure mind, and delighting in cultivating the immeasurable factors of the path—
this is the Dharma-delight of a bodhisattva.
Then Māra said to his daughters,
"I wish to return with you all to the celestial palace.
The daughters replied:
"We and this householder share a joy in the Dharma that we find most delightful; we no longer take pleasure in the delights of the five senses.
Māra said, "Householder, would you relinquish these women?"
"One who gives all that they possess to others is a bodhisattva.
Vimalakīrti said,
"I have already renounced it!"
"You may take them with you, so that all sentient beings may have their aspirations for the Dharma fulfilled.
Thereupon, the women asked Vimalakīrti,
"How shall we dwell in the palace of Māra?"
Vimalakīrti said: "Sisters!
There is a dharma-gate called the 'Inexhaustible Lamp'; you should study it."

The lamp of inexhaustibility is like this: for example, when a single lamp is used to light hundreds of thousands of lamps, all that was in darkness becomes bright, yet the light of the original lamp is never exhausted.
It is thus, sisters!

Now, when a single bodhisattva instructs and guides hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, his own resolve for that path is neither extinguished nor exhausted; rather, in accordance with the Dharma he preaches, he himself increases all wholesome dharmas. This is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp."

Although you dwell in the palace of Māra, by means of this lamp of inexhaustibility, you cause countless sons and daughters of heaven to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; thus, you repay the Buddha’s kindness and bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
At that time, the goddess bowed her head at the feet of Vimalakīrti and, returning with Māra to her palace, suddenly vanished.
World-Honored One!
Since Vimalakīrti possesses such sovereign spiritual power, wisdom, and eloquence, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to the elder’s son Śrītejas,
“Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Śrītejas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness. Why is this? Because—”

I recall that in the past, I personally established a great assembly of offerings within my father’s house, providing sustenance for all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, as well as various non-Buddhists, the poor, the lowly, the solitary, and beggars.
When the seven days had passed, Vimalakīrti entered the assembly and said to me:
"Son of a noble family!
A great assembly of giving should not be like the one you have arranged; it should be an assembly for the gift of Dharma. Of what use is this assembly of material gifts?"
I said: "Householder! What is meant by the assembly for the gift of Dharma?"
He replied:
"The Dharma-giving assembly is without before or after; it simultaneously makes offerings to all sentient beings—this is called the Dharma-giving assembly."
He asked: "What does this mean? [The Buddha] replied:
"It means that through bodhi, one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness."
To rescue sentient beings, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion;
to uphold the true Dharma, one gives rise to the mind of joy;
to encompass wisdom, one practices the mind of equanimity.
By gathering in those who are stingy and greedy, one gives rise to the dāna-pāramitā;
by transforming those who violate the precepts, one gives rise to the śīla-pāramitā;
by means of the dharma of non-self, one gives rise to the kṣānti-pāramitā.
By being free from the marks of body and mind, one gives rise to the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā);
by means of the mark of bodhi, one gives rise to the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā);
and by means of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), one gives rise to the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
They transform sentient beings while giving rise to emptiness;
they do not abandon conditioned phenomena while giving rise to signlessness;
they manifest birth while giving rise to wishlessness.
To uphold the True Dharma, they give rise to the power of skillful means;
to deliver sentient beings, they give rise to the four methods of attraction;
to respectfully serve all, they give rise to the method of eliminating arrogance.
Regarding one's body, life, and wealth, give rise to the three steadfast dharmas;
regarding the six recollections, give rise to the dharma of mindfulness;
regarding the six points of harmonious respect, give rise to a mind of sincerity and straightforwardness.
Practicing wholesome dharmas gives rise to a pure livelihood;
a pure and joyful mind gives rise to proximity with the noble ones;
not harboring hatred for others gives rise to a disciplined mind.
One arouses the profound resolve through the dharma of renunciation;
one arouses extensive learning by practicing according to what has been taught;
and one arouses dwelling in secluded places through the dharma of non-contention.
One gives rise to meditative seclusion by inclining toward the wisdom of the Buddha;
one gives rise to the stages of practice by liberating sentient beings from their bonds;
and one gives rise to meritorious karma by perfecting the primary and secondary marks and purifying the Buddha-fields.
Knowing the mental inclinations of all sentient beings and preaching the Dharma accordingly, they initiate the karma of wisdom;
knowing that all phenomena are neither to be grasped nor rejected, entering the gate of the single characteristic, they initiate the karma of insight;
severing all afflictions, all hindrances, and all unwholesome dharmas, they initiate all wholesome karmas.
By attaining all wisdom and all wholesome dharmas, one gives rise to all factors that assist the path to Buddhahood.
In this way, noble son,
this is the assembly of the gift of Dharma.
“If a bodhisattva dwells in this Dharma-giving assembly, they become a great donor and a field of merit for all the world.
“World-Honored One!
When Vimalakīrti spoke these words on the Dharma, two hundred people from among the assembly of brahmins all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, my mind attained purity, and I marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence!
I prostrated myself and paid homage at the feet of Vimalakīrti, immediately untying a necklace worth hundreds of thousands to offer him; however, he was unwilling to accept it.
I said: "Householder!
I pray that you will certainly accept it; give it as you wish."

Vimalakīrti then accepted the necklace, divided it into two portions, took one portion and gave it to the lowliest beggar in this assembly, and took the other portion and offered it to that Tathāgata Duṣprasaha.

The entire assembly beheld the Tathāgata Duṣpradharṣa of the land of Prabhāsa; they also saw the pearl necklace above that Buddha transform into a jeweled pavilion with four pillars, magnificently adorned on all four sides, yet without obstructing one another.
When Vimalakīrti had manifested these supernatural transformations, he spoke these words:

"If a donor gives with an impartial mind to even the lowliest beggar, regarding them as identical to the field of merit of the Tathāgata—without making distinctions, equalizing their great compassion, and seeking no karmic reward—this is what is called the perfection of the gift of Dharma."

"In this city, even the lowliest beggar, upon seeing this supernatural power and hearing what was said, gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness."

In this manner, each of these bodhisattvas spoke to the Buddha regarding their own past causes and conditions, recounting the words spoken by Vimalakīrti; they all said, "We are not fit to go there to inquire after his illness."
