Chapter Five: Mañjuśrī Inquires After His Illness At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
“Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That superior person is difficult to engage in dialogue with.”
He has profoundly penetrated the true nature of reality and is skilled in expounding the essential points of the Dharma; his eloquence is unimpeded and his wisdom is unhindered.
He fully understands all the ritual methods of the bodhisattvas and enters every secret treasury of the Buddhas.
Having subdued all demons, he sports with supernatural powers; in both wisdom and skillful means, he has already attained perfection.
"Nevertheless, we shall comply with the Buddha’s holy command and go there to inquire after his illness.
Thereupon, the various bodhisattvas, great disciples, Śakras, Brahmās, and the Four Heavenly Kings among the assembly all thought to themselves:
"Now that these two great beings, Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti, converse together, they will surely proclaim the sublime Dharma!"
Immediately, eight thousand bodhisattvas, five hundred śrāvakas, and hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all desired to follow him.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, surrounded and escorted with reverence by the assembly of bodhisattvas, great disciples, and devas and humans, entered the great city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti thought to himself,
"Now Mañjuśrī is coming with a great assembly!
He immediately employed his supernatural powers to empty the interior of his room, removing all furnishings as well as his attendants.
Only a single bed was set out, upon which he lay ill.
When Mañjuśrī entered his house, he saw that the room was empty and devoid of all possessions, with him alone reclining on the single bed.
Then Vimalakīrti said, "Welcome, Mañjuśrī!
You have come without the characteristic of coming; you have seen without the characteristic of seeing."
Mañjuśrī said: "So it is, householder!"
If it has already come, it will not come again;
if it has already gone, it will not go again. Why is this so?
That which comes comes from nowhere; that which goes goes nowhere. What can be seen cannot be seen again.
Set this matter aside, householder!
"Is this illness bearable?
Is there improvement from your treatment, and has it not worsened?
The World-Honored One sends his inquiries most earnestly and boundlessly."
"Householder!
What is the cause from which this illness arises?
How long has it been since it first appeared?"
"How should it be extinguished? Vimalakīrti replied,
"From ignorance and craving for existence, my illness arises."
Because all sentient beings are ill, I am ill;
if the illness of all sentient beings is extinguished, then my illness is extinguished. Why is this so?
For the sake of sentient beings, the bodhisattva enters into birth-and-death; where there is birth-and-death, there is illness.
If sentient beings can become free from illness, then the bodhisattva will no longer have illness.
It is like a householder who has an only son.
If that son falls ill, the parents also fall ill;
if the son recovers from his illness, the parents also recover.
In this way, the bodhisattva loves all sentient beings as if they were his own children.
When sentient beings are ill, the bodhisattva is ill;
when the illness of sentient beings is cured, the bodhisattva is also cured.
Furthermore, he asked, "From what cause does this illness arise?
Mañjuśrī replied, "The illness of a bodhisattva arises from great compassion. Mañjuśrī said:
“Householder!
Why is this room empty and devoid of attendants?
Vimalakīrti replied:
“The buddha-fields are likewise all empty.
He asked again:
“By what are they empty?”
He replied, "By means of the emptiness of emptiness.
He asked again:
"Of what use is emptiness?
Why is it empty? He replied:
"It is empty because it is the emptiness of non-discrimination."
He asked again:
"Can emptiness be conceptually differentiated?
He replied:
"Discrimination, too, is empty.
He asked again:
"Where should one seek emptiness?"
He replied,
“One should seek it among the sixty-two views.
He asked again:
"Where should the sixty-two views be sought?
He replied,
"They should be sought within the liberation of all Buddhas."
He asked again:
"Where should one seek the liberation of all Buddhas?
He replied:
"You should seek it within the mental activities of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding what you asked:
'Why do you have no attendant? [it is because...]"
"All maras and all heterodox teachers are my attendants. Why is this?
The maras delight in birth and death, yet the bodhisattva does not abandon birth and death."
"Non-Buddhists delight in various views, whereas Bodhisattvas remain unmoved by all views.
Mañjuśrī asked, "Householder, what is the nature of your illness?"
Vimalakīrti said,
"My illness is formless and invisible.
He asked again:
"Is this illness conjoined with the body,
or is it conjoined with the mind? He replied:
"It does not unite with the body, because the characteristics of the body are detached;
nor does it unite with the mind, because the mind is like an illusion.
He asked again:
“Regarding the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element—among these four elements, which element is afflicted by disease?
He replied:
“This disease is not the earth element, yet it is not separate from the earth element.”
The elements of water, fire, and wind are likewise.
Since the illnesses of sentient beings arise from these four great elements, because they have illness, I too am ill.
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti:
"How should a bodhisattva console a sick bodhisattva?
Vimalakīrti replied:
"He speaks of the body as impermanent, yet does not speak of wearying detachment from the body;
he speaks of the body as suffering, yet does not speak of delighting in nirvāṇa;
he speaks of the body as selfless, yet speaks of teaching and transforming sentient beings."
He speaks of the body as empty and quiescent, yet does not speak of ultimate extinction;
he speaks of repenting for past transgressions, yet does not speak of entering the past;
through his own illness, he takes pity on the illnesses of others.
One should recognize the suffering of countless kalpas in past lives; one should mindfully bring benefit to all sentient beings;
one should recollect the merit one has cultivated and attend to pure livelihood, not giving rise to anxiety or affliction, but constantly exerting diligence;
one should act as a King of Physicians to cure all manner of diseases.
“A bodhisattva should console a sick bodhisattva in this way, causing them to rejoice.
Mañjuśrī said, “Householder!
"How should a sick bodhisattva discipline his mind?
Vimalakīrti replied,
"A sick bodhisattva should reflect in this way:"
"This illness of mine now arises entirely from the delusions, inversions, and various afflictions of past lives; it has no substantial reality. Who, then, is there to suffer this illness?"
Why is this so? Because it is a combination of the four great elements that is conventionally designated as a "body";
since the four great elements have no master, the body likewise has no self.
"Furthermore, the arising of this illness is entirely due to attachment to a self; therefore, one should not give rise to attachment toward the self.
Having thus understood the root of the illness, one immediately eliminates the notion of a self and the notion of sentient beings.
One should give rise to the perception of phenomena (dharmasaṃjñā) and form this thought:
"This body is merely composed of a collection of phenomena;
its arising is only the arising of phenomena, and its cessation is only the cessation of phenomena."
"Furthermore, these phenomena do not know one another; when they arise, they do not say 'I am arising,' and when they cease, they do not say 'I am ceasing.
That sick bodhisattva, in order to eliminate the notion of phenomena, should form this thought:
'This notion of phenomena is also a perversion, and perversion is a great affliction; I should abandon it.'"
"What is meant by 'detachment'?
It is detachment from 'I' and 'mine.
What does it mean to be detached from 'I' and 'mine'?"
This refers to being free from two things.
What is meant by being free from two things?
It means not dwelling on the internal or external, but practicing all phenomena with equanimity.
What is meant by equality?
It means that the self is equal to nirvana. Why is this so?
Both "self" and "nirvāṇa"—these two are both empty.
By what are they empty?
They are empty merely by way of names.
These two dharmas lack any fixed nature; when one attains this equality, there is no further illness, only the illness of emptiness, and even that illness of emptiness is empty.

This sick bodhisattva experiences all sensations with a state of non-appropriation; yet, while not yet fully possessing the Buddha-dharma, he does not extinguish sensation to realize the fruit of enlightenment.
"Even if his body suffers pain, he contemplates sentient beings in the evil realms and gives rise to great compassion."
Having been tamed myself, I shall likewise tame all sentient beings;
I merely remove their illness without removing the phenomena themselves, teaching them in order to sever the root of that illness.
What is called the root of illness?
It is the existence of objective grasping (*ālambana*); from the existence of objective grasping, there arises the root of illness.
What is it that is grasped as an object?
These are called the three realms.
How does one sever攀緣 (pān-yuán, objective clinging)?
By means of non-apprehension; if there is no apprehension, then there is no clinging.
What is meant by "non-apprehension"?
It means being free from the two views—what are the two views?
They are the internal view and the external view; this is non-apprehension.
Mañjuśrī! This is how a sick bodhisattva disciplines the mind; it is for the sake of severing the suffering of old age, sickness, and death—this is the bodhi of that bodhisattva.
If it were not thus, what one has cultivated and refined would be without the benefit of wisdom.
Just as one who conquers an enemy may be called brave,
so too is one who simultaneously eliminates old age, sickness, and death called a Bodhisattva.
"That sick Bodhisattva should further reflect thus:"
"Just as my own illness is neither real nor existent, so too the illnesses of all sentient beings are neither real nor existent.
When making this contemplation, if one gives rise to a great compassion based on attachment or views toward sentient beings, one should immediately abandon it.

Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas eliminate adventitious afflictions and give rise to great compassion; those whose compassion is rooted in attachment and views will experience weariness and exhaustion within birth and death.
If they can remain free from these, they will have no weariness or exhaustion, and in whatever place they are born, they will not be obscured by attachment and views.
That which is born is without bondage; yet it can preach the Dharma for sentient beings to liberate them from their bonds, as the Buddha has said:
"It is impossible that one who is themselves bound could liberate others from their bonds;
it is possible that one who is themselves unbound could liberate others from their bonds."
Therefore, a bodhisattva should not give rise to bondage.
What is called bondage?
What is called liberation?
To be attached to the flavor of meditative concentration is the bondage of a bodhisattva;
to be born through skillful means is the liberation of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, wisdom without skillful means is bondage, while wisdom with skillful means is liberation.
Bondage consists of wisdom without skillful means; liberation consists of wisdom with skillful means.
What is meant by bondage of wisdom without skillful means?
It refers to a bodhisattva who, with a mind of attachment and views, adorns buddha-fields and brings sentient beings to maturity.
To discipline oneself within the states of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness is called "bondage by wisdom lacking skillful means.
What is meant by "liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means"?

This means not adorning buddha-fields or bringing sentient beings to maturity with a mind of craving or views; rather, within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one practices self-discipline without weariness—this is called liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means.
What is called the bondage of lacking skillful means?
It refers to a bodhisattva who, while dwelling amidst afflictions such as greed, anger, and wrong views, plants the roots of various virtues; this is called the bondage of lacking skillful means.
What is meant by "liberation through wisdom and skillful means"?

It refers to being free from all afflictions such as greed, anger, and false views, while planting the roots of various virtues and dedicating them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is called liberation through wisdom and skillful means.
Mañjuśrī! That sick bodhisattva should contemplate all phenomena in this way.

Furthermore, contemplating that the body is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self is called wisdom (*prajñā*). Although the body is ill, remaining constantly within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to benefit all beings without weariness is called skillful means (*upāya*).

Furthermore, one contemplates the body: the body is not separate from illness, and illness is not separate from the body. This illness and this body are neither new nor old; this is called wisdom (*prajñā*). Even if the body has an ailment, it is not eternally extinguished; this is called skillful means (*upāya*).
“Mañjuśrī! A sick bodhisattva should thus discipline his mind, neither dwelling within it, nor dwelling in an undisciplined mind.”
Why is this? If one dwells in an undisciplined mind, that is the way of fools;
if one dwells in a disciplined mind, that is the way of the śrāvakas.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should not abide in a mind that is either disciplined or undisciplined; to be free from these two dharmas is the practice of a bodhisattva.
To remain within birth and death without being defiled by conduct, and to abide in nirvana without entering final extinction—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
It is not the practice of ordinary beings, nor the practice of noble sages; it is the practice of Bodhisattvas.
It is not a defiled practice, nor a pure practice; it is the practice of Bodhisattvas.
Although they have transcended the practices of Māra, they manifest the subduing of all Māras; this is the practice of Bodhisattvas.
To seek all-knowledge without seeking at an improper time is the practice of a bodhisattva;
though observing that all phenomena are unarisen, not entering the stage of certainty is the practice of a bodhisattva;
though observing the twelve links of dependent origination, entering into various false views is the practice of a bodhisattva.
To embrace all sentient beings without attachment is the practice of a bodhisattva;
to delight in seclusion without relying on the exhaustion of body and mind is the practice of a bodhisattva;
to traverse the three realms without destroying the nature of phenomena is the practice of a bodhisattva.
To practice within emptiness while planting the roots of all virtues is the bodhisattva’s practice;
to practice within signlessness while delivering sentient beings is the bodhisattva’s practice;
to practice within wishlessness while manifesting the reception of a body is the bodhisattva’s practice.
To practice without arising, yet to give rise to all wholesome deeds, is the bodhisattva practice;
to practice the six pāramitās, yet to fully know the minds and mental factors of sentient beings, is the bodhisattva practice;
to practice the six supernormal powers, yet not to exhaust the outflows, is the bodhisattva practice.
To practice the four immeasurable minds without craving or attachment to rebirth in the Brahma world is the bodhisattva’s practice;
to practice dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi without being born according to those meditative states is the bodhisattva’s practice;
to practice the four foundations of mindfulness without permanently abandoning the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena is the bodhisattva’s practice.
To practice the four right efforts while not abandoning physical and mental diligence is the bodhisattva practice;
to practice the four bases of power while attaining sovereign supernormal powers is the bodhisattva practice;
to practice the five faculties while discerning the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings is the bodhisattva practice.
To practice the five powers while joyfully seeking the ten powers of a Buddha is the conduct of a bodhisattva;
to practice the seven factors of enlightenment while discerning the wisdom of a Buddha is the conduct of a bodhisattva;
to practice the eightfold noble path while joyfully practicing the immeasurable path of a Buddha is the conduct of a bodhisattva.
To practice the methods that assist the path through both calm abiding and insight, yet not ultimately fall into cessation, is the conduct of a bodhisattva;
to practice that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, yet to adorn one’s body with the primary and secondary marks, is the conduct of a bodhisattva;
to manifest the deportment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, yet not abandon the Buddha-dharma, is the conduct of a bodhisattva.
To accord with the ultimately pure characteristics of all phenomena while manifesting a body according to what is appropriate is the practice of a bodhisattva;
to contemplate that all buddha-lands are eternally quiescent like space while manifesting various kinds of pure buddha-lands is the practice of a bodhisattva;
and to attain the path of the Buddha, turn the wheel of Dharma, and enter nirvana, yet not abandon the path of a bodhisattva, is the practice of a bodhisattva.
When these words were spoken, eight thousand devaputras from among the great assembly led by Mañjuśrī all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Chapter Six: The Inconceivable At that time, Śāriputra, seeing that there were no seats within this room, had this thought:
"Where shall these bodhisattvas and the great assembly of disciples sit?"
The elder Vimalakīrti, knowing his thoughts, said to Śāriputra:
"What do you think, worthy one?
Have you come for the sake of the Dharma?"
"Are you seeking a seat?
Śāriputra replied,
"I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of a seat."
Vimalakīrti said, "Yes,
Śāriputra! One who seeks the Dharma does not cling even to body or life, much less to a seat."

Now, one who seeks the Dharma does not seek it in form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; does not seek it in the elements or the sense bases; and does not seek it in the realms of desire, form, or formlessness.
"O Śāriputra! One who seeks the Dharma does not seek by attachment to the Buddha, does not seek by attachment to the Dharma, and does not seek by attachment to the Saṅgha.
One who seeks the Dharma has no seeking that views suffering, no seeking that abandons the origin [of suffering], and no seeking that realizes cessation or cultivates the path."

Why is this? Because the Dharma is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). If one says, "I shall see suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path," this is conceptual proliferation and not the pursuit of the Dharma.
"O Śāriputra! The Dharma is named 'quiescence.
If one practices with arising and ceasing, this is seeking arising and ceasing, not seeking the Dharma.
The Dharma is named 'stainless. If one becomes defiled by dharmas, even up to nirvāṇa, this is attachment; it is not seeking the Dharma."
The Dharma has no place for practice; if one practices within the Dharma, that is a place of practice, not the seeking of the Dharma.
The Dharma is without taking or rejecting; if one takes up or rejects the Dharma, that is taking and rejecting, not the seeking of the Dharma.
The Dharma has no location; if one clings to a location, that is clinging to a location, not the seeking of the Dharma.
The Dharma is called signless; if one follows signs with consciousness, this is seeking signs rather than seeking the Dharma.
The Dharma cannot be dwelt upon; if one dwells in the Dharma, this is dwelling in the Dharma rather than seeking the Dharma.
The Dharma cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known; if one acts through seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, this is seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing rather than seeking the Dharma.
The Dharma is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). If one practices the conditioned, one is seeking the conditioned and not seeking the Dharma.
Therefore, Śāriputra, if one seeks the Dharma, one should seek nothing at all regarding any phenomena.
When these words were spoken, five hundred devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī, "Virtuous one, you travel through immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya lands; in which Buddha-field is there a lion throne endowed with such excellent, sublime, and accomplished merits?"
Mañjuśrī said, “Householder!
To the east, beyond thirty-six Ganges-sands of worlds, there is a world named Sumeru-lakṣaṇa. Its Buddha is named Sumeru-dīpa-rāja, and he currently resides there.”
That Buddha’s body was eighty-four thousand yojanas in height, and his lion throne was eighty-four thousand yojanas high, the most exquisitely adorned of all.

Thereupon, the elder Vimalakīrti manifested his supernormal powers, and immediately that Buddha dispatched thirty-two thousand lion thrones—lofty, broad, magnificent, and pure—which entered the room of Vimalakīrti; these had never before been seen by the bodhisattvas, great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, the four heavenly kings, and the others.
The chamber was vast and spacious, fully accommodating all thirty-two thousand lion thrones without any obstruction.
Neither the city of Vaiśālī nor Jambudvīpa, nor the four continents, were cramped; all appeared exactly as they had before.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Mañjuśrī,
“Take your place upon the lion throne!
Sit together with these superior bodhisattvas, and you should manifest your own body in accordance with the form of this seat.”

The bodhisattva who had attained supernatural powers immediately transformed his own body to a height of forty-two thousand yojanas and sat upon a lion throne; none of the bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds, nor any of the great disciples, were able to ascend it.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra,
"Take your seat upon the lion throne!
Śāriputra replied:
“Householder!
This seat is high and wide; I cannot ascend it.
Vimalakīrti said:
"Indeed, Śāriputra!
Only by prostrating before the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja can you sit.
Thereupon, the bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds and the great disciples immediately prostrated before the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja and were able to sit upon the lion thrones.
Śāriputra said: "Householder!
This is truly unprecedented!"

Thus, this small room can accommodate these high and vast seats without obstructing the city of Vaiśālī; furthermore, it does not crowd the villages, towns, and cities of Jambudvīpa, nor the palaces of the devas, nāga kings, and spirits throughout the four continents.
Vimalakīrti said: "Indeed, Śāriputra!
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess a liberation called 'inconceivable.'"

If a bodhisattva dwells in this liberation, they can place the height and breadth of Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed without any increase or decrease; yet the primary characteristics of the King of Mountains, Sumeru, remain as they were. The Four Heavenly Kings and the various gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven neither perceive nor know where they have entered. Only those who are ready for deliverance see Mount Sumeru enter into the mustard seed. This is called dwelling in the inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation.

Furthermore, he takes the waters of the four great oceans and places them within a single pore, yet he does not disturb the fish, turtles, tortoises, crocodiles, or any other aquatic creatures; the great ocean remains as it was in its original state, and the dragons, spirits, and asuras do not perceive or know where they have been placed, nor is there any disturbance to these beings.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who dwells in this inconceivable liberation can take up the trichiliocosm as if it were a potter’s wheel, place it upon his right palm, and hurl it beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; yet the sentient beings therein are neither aware nor do they know where they have gone.
He then returns it to its original location, causing no one to perceive any coming or going, while the world remains exactly as it was before.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there are sentient beings who delight in remaining long in the world and can be delivered, the Bodhisattva immediately extends seven days to constitute one kalpa, causing those sentient beings to perceive it as one kalpa;

if there are sentient beings who do not delight in remaining long and can be delivered, the Bodhisattva immediately contracts one kalpa to constitute seven days, causing those sentient beings to perceive it as seven days.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva dwelling in the inconceivable liberation can gather the adornments of all buddha-fields into a single land and manifest them to sentient beings.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva places the sentient beings of a single buddha-field upon his right palm and flies to the ten directions to display them everywhere, yet without moving them from their original location.
Moreover, Śāriputra!
The Bodhisattva causes all sentient beings of the ten directions to see, within a single pore, all the offerings presented to the Buddhas;
furthermore, he causes them to universally behold all the suns, moons, and stars existing throughout the lands of the ten directions, within that same single pore.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

All the winds existing throughout the worlds of the ten directions, a bodhisattva is able to inhale and draw into his mouth, yet his body suffers no injury, nor are the trees outside broken or shattered;

furthermore, when the kalpa of the ten directions is consumed by fire at its end, he can place all those fires within his belly, and the fires continue their work as before without causing him any harm.

Furthermore, from below, he takes a buddha-field beyond as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges and places it above, past as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, as easily as one might pick up a jujube leaf with the point of a needle, without causing it any disturbance.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation can, by means of supernormal powers, manifest the body of a Buddha, or manifest the body of a pratyekabuddha, or manifest the body of a śrāvaka, or manifest the body of Śakra, or manifest the body of Brahmā, or manifest the body of a world-protector, or manifest the body of a wheel-turning monarch.

Furthermore, all sounds existing throughout the worlds of the ten directions—whether superior, middling, or inferior—they are able to transform them all into the voice of the Buddha, producing the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, as well as the various teachings expounded by the Buddhas of the ten directions, so that all may hear them universally therein.
“Śāriputra!
I have now briefly described the power of the bodhisattvas’ inconceivable liberation; were it to be explained in detail, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, having heard this teaching on the bodhisattvas’ inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and said to Śāriputra:
"It is, for example, like a person who displays various forms and images before someone who is blind; they cannot see them.
It is just so with all śrāvakas who hear this inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation—they are unable to understand it."
Upon hearing this, what wise person would not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Why have we forever severed our roots, becoming like spoiled seeds regarding this Mahāyāna?
When all the śrāvakas hear this inconceivable Dharma-door of liberation, they should all weep aloud, their voices shaking the trichiliocosm;
all the bodhisattvas should rejoice greatly and receive this Dharma upon the crowns of their heads.
"If there are bodhisattvas who have faith and understanding in this inconceivable Dharma-gate of liberation, no host of Māras can do anything to them.
When Mahākāśyapa had spoken these words, thirty-two thousand devaputras all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Mahākāśyapa:
"Venerable one!
Among those who act as Māras in the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions, most are bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation."
By the power of skillful means, they teach and transform sentient beings by manifesting as Māra kings.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, there may be those among the immeasurable bodhisattvas of the ten directions who beg from others for their hands, feet, ears, noses, heads, eyes, marrow, brains, blood, flesh, skin, bones, villages, cities, wives, children, male and female slaves, elephants, horses, carriages, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, *śaṅkha*, coral, amber, pearls, conch shells, clothing, food, or drink. Such beggars are mostly bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation who, through the power of skillful means, go to test them so as to make their resolve firm.

Why is this so? Because a bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation possesses the power of majestic virtue; therefore, they manifest acts of oppression to demonstrate such difficult matters to all sentient beings.
Ordinary persons are inferior and lack such power and influence that they could ever oppress a bodhisattva in this way.
It is like the trampling of a dragon-elephant, which a donkey cannot endure.
This is called the gate of wisdom and skillful means of a bodhisattva who dwells in inconceivable liberation.
Chapter Seven: Contemplating Sentient Beings In the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, Chapter Seven: Contemplating Sentient Beings. At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti:
"How does a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings?"
Vimalakīrti said: "For example, just as a magician perceives the person created by his magic, so does a bodhisattva perceive sentient beings.

It is like a wise man seeing the moon in water; like seeing one's own reflection in a mirror; like a mirage in the heat; like an echo; like clouds in the sky; like foam on the water; like bubbles on the surface of the water; like the solidity of a plantain tree; like lightning remaining for a long time; like a fifth great element; like a sixth aggregate; like a seventh sense-organ; like a thirteenth base; like a nineteenth realm—so does a bodhisattva perceive sentient beings."

As form in the formless realm; as the sprout of parched grain; as the view of a self-body in a stream-enterer; as the entry into a womb by a non-returner; as the three poisons in an arhat; as greed, anger, and breaking of precepts in a bodhisattva who has attained forbearance; as the residual habit-energies of afflictions in a Buddha; as seeing forms by one who is blind; as inhalation and exhalation in one who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation; as the tracks of a bird in the sky; as the son of a barren woman; as the arising of afflictions in a magically created person; as the seeing of things in a dream after having awakened; as the taking up of a body by one who has entered parinirvāṇa; and as fire without smoke—in this manner does a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī said, “If a bodhisattva practices contemplation in this manner, how does he practice loving-kindness?
Vimalakīrti replied:
"Once the bodhisattva has made this contemplation, he thinks to himself:
'I shall preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
This is precisely true compassion."
One practices the compassion of quiescence because there is nothing that arises;
one practices the compassion free from fever because there are no afflictions;
one practices impartial compassion because it is equal throughout the three periods of time.
He practices the compassion of non-contention because nothing arises;
he practices the compassion of non-duality because the internal and external do not meet;
he practices the compassion of indestructibility because it is ultimately exhausted.
One practices steadfast compassion because the mind is indestructible;
one practices pure compassion because the nature of all phenomena is pure;
one practices boundless compassion because it is like space.
One practices the compassion of an arhat because it destroys the thieves of the fetters;
one practices the compassion of a bodhisattva because it brings peace to sentient beings;
one practices the compassion of a Tathāgata because it realizes the mark of suchness.
One practices the compassion of a Buddha because it awakens sentient beings;
one practices spontaneous compassion because it is attained without cause;
one practices the compassion of bodhi because it is of a single, equal flavor.
They practice peerless compassion, for they have severed all craving;
they practice great compassionate love, for they guide others by means of the Mahāyāna;
they practice tireless compassion, for they contemplate emptiness and non-self.
They practice the compassion of the gift of Dharma because they leave nothing behind out of stinginess;
they practice the compassion of upholding the precepts because they transform those who violate the prohibitions;
they practice the compassion of patience because they protect both self and others.
One practices the compassion of diligence because one bears the burden of sentient beings;
one practices the compassion of meditative concentration because one does not relish its flavor;
one practices the compassion of wisdom because there is nothing for which the proper time is not known.
They practice the compassion of skillful means because they manifest everything;
they practice the compassion of non-concealment because their straightforward mind is pure;
they practice the compassion of the profound mind because their conduct is unmixed.
He practices the compassion of non-deception, because it is not false or artificial;
he practices the compassion of peace and happiness, because it causes others to attain the bliss of a Buddha.
Such is the compassion of a bodhisattva.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"What is meant by compassion?
He replied:
"Whatever meritorious deeds a bodhisattva performs, he shares them all with all sentient beings.
"What is meant by 'joy'?
He replied:
"To have benefited others, and to feel joy without regret.
"What is meant by 'equanimity'?
He replied:
“Regarding the merit and blessings performed, there is no expectation of reward.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
“In the terrors of birth and death, upon what should a bodhisattva rely?”
Vimalakīrti said,
"When a bodhisattva is amidst the fear of birth and death, they should rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
“If a bodhisattva wishes to rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits, in what should they abide?
He replied:
“A bodhisattva who wishes to rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits should abide in the liberation of all sentient beings.”
He asked again:
"If one wishes to deliver sentient beings, what should be eliminated?
He replied:
"I wish to deliver sentient beings by removing their afflictions.
He asked again:
"To remove afflictions, what should one practice?"
He replied,
“One should practice right mindfulness.
He asked again:
"What is meant by practicing right mindfulness?
He replied:
"One should practice that which is neither arising nor ceasing."
He asked again:
"What dharma does not arise?
What dharma does not cease?"
He replied,
“The unwholesome does not arise, and wholesome dharmas do not cease.
He asked again:
“What is the root of the wholesome and the unwholesome?
He replied:
“The body is the root.”
He asked again:
"What is the root of the body?
He replied:
“Sensual desire is the root.
He asked again:
“What is the root of sensual desire?”
He replied:
"False conceptualization is the root.
He asked again:
"What is the root of false discrimination?
He replied,
"Perverted perception is its root."
He asked again:
"What is the root of inverted perception?
He replied:
"Non-abiding is the foundation.
He asked again,
"What is the foundation of non-abiding?"
He replied:
"If there is no abiding, then there is no root. Mañjuśrī!"
"From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.

At that time, there was a goddess in the room of Vimalakīrti who, seeing these great beings and hearing the Dharma they had preached, manifested her form and immediately scattered celestial flowers over the bodhisattvas and the great disciples.
When the flowers reached the various bodhisattvas, they all fell away; but when they reached the great disciples, they stuck and did not fall.
Although all the disciples used their supernatural powers to remove the flowers, they could not make them go.
At that time, the goddess asked Śāriputra,
"For what reason do you remove these flowers?
He replied:
"These flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma; therefore, I have removed them.
The deva said, "Do not say that these flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma."
Why is this? These flowers are devoid of discrimination; it is you, O virtuous one, who give rise to the notion of discrimination!
If one has gone forth in the Buddha-dharma and harbors such discrimination, it is contrary to the Dharma.
If there is no conceptual discrimination, this is in accordance with the Dharma.
Observe that the flowers do not adhere to the bodhisattvas because they have already severed all conceptualizations.
It is like when a person is afraid; non-humans find an opportunity to take advantage of them.
Thus, because such disciples fear birth and death, form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch gain the advantage over them.
For one who has already abandoned fear, none of the five desires can do anything;
yet as long as their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, the flowers will merely adhere to their bodies.
"When the habit-energies of fetters are exhausted, the flower does not adhere.
Śāriputra said,
"How long has it been since the goddess stayed in this room?"
He replied,
"I dwell in this room as one who has attained liberation,
O Elder. Śāriputra said:
"Have you been here for a long time?
The deva replied,
"How long has it been since the Elder attained liberation?"
Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer.
The goddess said,
"Why do you, an elder of great wisdom, remain silent?"
He replied, "Liberation is beyond all verbal expression; therefore, I do not know what to say about it.
The deva said:
“Words and letters are all the marks of liberation. Why is this?
Liberation is neither internal nor external, nor does it abide in between the two.”
Syllables are neither internal nor external,
nor do they exist in between. Therefore, Śāriputra,
one does not speak of liberation apart from syllables.
"Why is this? Because all dharmas have the characteristic of liberation.
Śāriputra said:
"Is it not the case that one is liberated by being free from lust, anger, and delusion?
The deva replied,
"The Buddha spoke of liberation through freedom from lust, anger, and delusion only for those with overweening pride."
"If one is free from overweening pride, the Buddha says that the very nature of lust, anger,
and delusion is itself liberation. Śāriputra said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Devī! What have you attained?
By what do you realize it?"
"Your eloquence is indeed such as this!
The deva said, "I have neither attainment nor realization; therefore, my eloquence is such as this."
"Why is this? If there were anyone who attained or realized [anything], they would be considered arrogant regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Śāriputra asked the goddess:
"In which of the three vehicles do you aspire?
The deva replied,
"Because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of the śrāvakas, I am a śrāvaka."
Because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of causes and conditions, I am a pratyekabuddha;
because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of great compassion, I am the Mahāyāna. Śāriputra!
Just as when a person enters a campaka grove, they smell only the campaka and do not smell any other fragrance,
so too, if one enters this room, one smells only the fragrance of the Buddha’s merits and does not delight in smelling the fragrance of the merits of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Śāriputra! Whenever Śakras, Brahmās, the Four Heavenly Kings, or any among the devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and others enter this room, they hear this superior person expounding the True Dharma; having all come to delight in the fragrance of the Buddha’s merits, they resolve their minds [for enlightenment] before departing.

Śāriputra! I have resided in this room for twelve years, yet from the beginning I have never heard the Dharma of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; I have heard only the Bodhisattvas’ great kindness and great compassion, and the inconceivable Dharmas of all Buddhas.
Śāriputra! In this room, eight extraordinary and rare dharmas are constantly manifested.
What are these eight?

This room is constantly illuminated by golden light, with no difference between day and night; it does not rely on the illumination of the sun or moon for its brightness—this is the first unprecedented and rare quality.
Those who enter this room are not afflicted by any defilements—this is the second unprecedented and rare quality.
This room is always filled with an unceasing assembly of Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Bodhisattvas from other directions—this is the third unprecedented and rare quality.
In this chamber, the Dharma of the six *pāramitās* and non-retrogression is constantly preached; this is the fourth rare and unprecedented phenomenon.

In this chamber, the supreme music of devas and humans is perpetually performed, and from its strings emerge infinite sounds of Dharma-transformations; this is the fifth rare and unprecedented phenomenon.

In this chamber there are four great treasuries, filled to overflowing with various jewels, which provide for the destitute and relieve the needy, yielding inexhaustibly upon request; this is the sixth rare and unprecedented phenomenon.

In this room, Śākyamuni Buddha, Amitābha Buddha, Akṣobhya Buddha, Ratnaguṇa, Ratnārcis, Ratnacandra, Ratnavyūha, Durjaya, Siṃhanāda, Sarvārthasiddha, and other such infinite Buddhas of the ten directions—whenever this noble person brings them to mind, they all immediately come, extensively expound the secret and essential Dharma-treasures of the Buddhas, and having finished speaking, depart; this is the seventh unprecedented and rare quality.
Furthermore, within this room, the adorned palaces of all the devas and the pure lands of all the Buddhas appear therein; this is the eighth unprecedented and rare quality.
Śāriputra! In this room, eight extraordinary and rare dharmas are constantly manifested. Who, having seen such inconceivable matters, would still take pleasure in the Dharma of the śrāvakas?
Śāriputra said,
"Why do you not transform your female body?
The goddess replied:
"For twelve years now, I have sought the mark of a woman and found it utterly non-existent; how then could there be any transformation?
It is like a magician who conjures an illusory woman, and someone asks:
'Why do you not transform this female body?'"
"Would this person be asking correctly?
Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"An illusion has no fixed characteristic; what, then, could it transform?
The goddess said, "All dharmas are likewise thus: they have no fixed characteristics. Why, then, do you ask why she does not transform her female body?"
Immediately, the goddess used her supernatural powers to transform Śāriputra so that he appeared like a goddess, while she herself transformed her body to appear like Śāriputra, and asked:
"Why do you not transform this female body?"
Śāriputra, assuming the form of a goddess, replied:
"I do not know by what transformation I have changed into this female body.
The goddess said:
“Śāriputra! If you can transform this female body, then all women should likewise be able to transform theirs.
Just as you, Śāriputra, are not a woman yet manifest in a female body, so it is with all women; though they manifest in female bodies, they are not women.”
"Therefore, the Buddha has taught that all dharmas are neither male nor female.
Immediately, the goddess withdrew her supernatural power, and Śāriputra’s body returned to its former state.
The Deva asked Śāriputra,
"Where now is the physical form and appearance of your female body?
Śāriputra replied:
“The physical form and characteristics of a woman’s body neither exist nor do not exist.
The deva said, “All dharmas are likewise thus; they neither exist nor do not exist.”
"That which neither exists nor does not exist is what the Buddha has taught.
Śāriputra asked the goddess,
"When you pass away from here, where will you be reborn?"
The deva said:
"I am born just as that which is produced through the Buddha's transformation.
He asked:
"The Buddha is produced through transformation; he does not undergo death and rebirth.
The deva said, "It is the same for all sentient beings: there is no death and rebirth."
Śāriputra asked the goddess,
“After how long will you attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The goddess replied:
"If Śāriputra were to return to being an ordinary person, only then would I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra said, "That I should become an ordinary person— such a thing is impossible."
The deva said:
"That I should attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment is likewise impossible. Why is this so?

The deva said:

"By virtue of his original vows, he is able to manifest himself at will to teach and transform sentient beings.

He asked again:

"If a bodhisattva practices the five deeds of immediate retribution yet remains free from affliction and anger;..."
Reaching the hells, they are free from all defilements of sin;
reaching the animal realm, they are free from faults such as ignorance and arrogance;
reaching the realm of hungry ghosts, they are fully endowed with merit and virtue.

He manifests the practice of anger, yet is always compassionate and patient;

he manifests the practice of a distracted mind, yet is constantly mindful of meditative concentration.

they manifest entry into the realm of Māra, yet they accord with the Buddha’s wisdom and do not follow the teachings of others;

“Mañjuśrī! When a bodhisattva can practice in this way within what is not the path, this is called penetrating the Buddha-way.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī:

"To put it briefly, the sixty-two views and all afflictions are all the seeds of the Buddha.
[The interlocutor] asked: "What do you mean?"

It is like this: lotus flowers do not grow on high ground or dry land; they grow only in low-lying, damp mud."

Thus, those who perceive unconditioned dharmas and enter the stage of correctness can never again give rise to the Buddha-dharma; it is only within the mire of afflictions that sentient beings can bring forth the Buddha-dharma!
Furthermore, just as seeds sown in the air will never sprout, while in soil enriched with manure they can flourish;

likewise, those who have entered the station of the unconditioned do not give rise to the Buddha-dharma. Yet, even one who gives rise to a view of self as vast as Mount Sumeru is still able to produce the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and give birth to the Buddha-dharma!
Therefore, you should know that all afflictions constitute the seed of the Tathāgata.
Just as one cannot obtain a priceless jewel without descending into the great ocean,
so too one cannot obtain the jewel of omniscience without entering the great ocean of afflictions.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa exclaimed in praise:

"Speak these words quickly!
It is truly as you have said: the categories of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) constitute the lineage of the Tathāgata.

We are no longer capable of resolving to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; yet even those who have committed the five sins of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) can still conceive the aspiration to arise within the Buddha-dharma, whereas we, at present, can never conceive it."
Just as a man whose sense organs are destroyed can no longer derive benefit from the five objects of desire;
so too, a śrāvaka who has severed all fetters has nothing further to gain within the Buddha-dharma and will never again set his aspirations thereon.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, ordinary persons possess a sense of reciprocity toward the Buddha-dharma, whereas śrāvakas do not. Why is this so?
When ordinary beings hear the Buddha-dharma, they are able to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment and ensure that the Three Jewels are not severed;

even if Śrāvakas were to hear the Buddha-dharma, the [ten] powers, the [four] fearlessnesses, and so forth for the rest of their lives, they would never be able to generate the intention for unsurpassed enlightenment.

“Where have all the slaves, servants, elephants, horses, and carriages gone?
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti replied with a verse:

All guides of the multitudes arise from this;
Taking the joy of Dharma as one’s wife, The mind of compassion as one’s daughter,
A virtuous and sincere heart as one’s son, And ultimate emptiness and stillness as one’s home.
The assembly of disciples and their various afflictions turn according to the will [of the Bodhisattva];
the factors of enlightenment and spiritual friends thereby bring about the attainment of perfect awakening.
The various perfections are his equal companions, and the four means of integration are his female attendants.
Chanting and reciting the words of the Dharma— this constitutes their music.
The park of dhāraṇīs, the forest trees of the outflow-free Dharma,
the pure and wondrous flowers of the factors of enlightenment, and the fruits of liberation and wisdom.
The bathing pool of the eight liberations is filled with the limpid waters of meditative concentration;
strewn with the flowers of the seven purities, it bathes those people free from defilement.
With the five supernormal powers as their swift elephants and horses, they take the Great Vehicle as their chariot.
Tamed by a single mind, he wanders upon the Eightfold Path;
Adorned with the marks, his countenance is majestic; The grace of the secondary signs embellishes his form;
Shame and remorse are his noble raiment, And the profound mind is his floral garland.
Possessing the seven treasures of wealth, one causes them to increase through instruction;
practicing according to what has been taught and dedicating the merit for the sake of great benefit—
taking the four dhyānas as one’s bed and seat, these arise from pure livelihood.
Abundant learning increases wisdom; let this be your own voice of awakening.
The Dharma of ambrosia is your food, and the flavor of liberation is your drink.
Bathe with a pure mind, and take the precepts as your fragrant unguent.
Having utterly destroyed the thieves of affliction, He is courageous and invincible;
having subdued the four Māras, He raises the banner of victory at the site of enlightenment.
Though he knows there is neither arising nor ceasing, He manifests birth for the sake of others.
They manifest in all lands, just as the sun leaves nothing unseen.
They make offerings to the immeasurable billions of Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions;
regarding these Buddhas and their own bodies, they harbor no thought of discrimination.
Although they know that all Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty,
they constantly cultivate pure lands to transform and guide the multitudes of living beings.
Regarding all classes of sentient beings— their forms, sounds, and modes of deportment— [they understand them all].
The Bodhisattva Fearless Power can manifest all things at once.
Aware of the deeds of all Māras, he displays himself by following their ways;
through the wisdom of skillful means, he can manifest anything according to his will.
Sometimes they manifest old age, sickness, and death to bring all sentient beings to maturity;
understanding that these are like illusions and transformations, they attain unimpeded mastery.
Sometimes they manifest the conflagration at the end of an eon, wherein heaven and earth are utterly incinerated.
The multitude harbors the notion of permanence; he illuminates them so they may know impermanence.
Countless billions of sentient beings all come together to invite the Bodhisattva;
arriving at his dwelling at once, he transforms them and leads them toward the Buddha-way.
Whether it be the scriptures, incantations, and arts, or the various crafts and skills,
they manifest the practice of all these to benefit all living beings.
Regarding the many paths and dharmas of the world, they renounce the home life within them all.
Thereby resolving the delusions of people, so that they do not fall into false views.
Sometimes he becomes a sun or moon deity, or Brahmā, the Lord of the World;
sometimes he becomes earth or water, and again, he becomes wind or fire.
In kalpas of pestilence, he manifests as various medicinal herbs;
those who consume them are cured of illness and their many toxins are eliminated.
In kalpas of famine, he manifests in bodily form as food and drink.
First one rescues them from hunger and thirst, and subsequently instructs people with the Dharma;
when there are weapons and warfare in an eon, one gives rise to a heart of compassion for them,
transforming all those sentient beings and causing them to abide in the ground of non-contention.
If there is a great battle array, he establishes it with equal strength;
the Bodhisattva manifests his majestic power to subdue them and bring about peace and harmony.
Throughout all lands, in every place where there are hells—
I immediately go to those places to strive to rescue them from their suffering;
throughout all lands where animals devour one another,
I manifest birth among them all to bring them benefit.
Manifesting the experience of the five desires, yet also appearing to practice dhyāna,
he causes the mind of Māra to be confounded and disordered, so that Māra cannot find an opportunity.
To produce a lotus flower amidst fire— this may be called truly rare.
To practice dhyāna while remaining in the realm of desire is likewise rare and marvelous.
Sometimes they manifest as courtesans to attract those who lust after beauty;
first drawing them in with the hook of desire, they later lead them into the Buddha-way.
Sometimes acting as a leader of a village, or serving as a guide for merchants,
or as a national preceptor and high minister, they bring benefit and aid to sentient beings.
To all those who are poor and destitute, they manifest as an inexhaustible treasury.
I therefore exhorted them, causing them to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
To those whose minds were arrogant, I manifested as a great strongman to subdue their pride and cause them to abide in the Unsurpassed Way.
For those who are fearful, he stands before them to offer comfort;
first bestowing fearlessness upon them, he later causes them to resolve for the Way.
Or he manifests as one free from lustful desire, becoming a seer endowed with the five supernatural powers.
He guides and instructs all living beings, causing them to abide in precepts, patience, and loving-kindness.
When he sees those who require service, he manifests as their servant;
having gladdened their hearts, he then inspires in them the mind of the Way.
According to whatever they require, they may enter the Buddha-way;
by the power of skillful means, he is able to provide for them all sufficiently.
Thus the Way is immeasurable, and that which is practiced has no limit.
His wisdom is boundless, delivering countless multitudes.
Even if all Buddhas were to praise his meritorious virtues for immeasurable billions of kalpas, they still could not exhaust them.
Who, having heard such a Dharma as this, would not resolve upon Bodhicitta?
Except for those unworthy persons, who are deluded, ignorant, and lacking wisdom.
Chapter Nine: Entering the Gate of Non-Duality From the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra At that time, Vimalakīrti addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
“Virtuous ones!
How does a bodhisattva enter the gate of non-duality?
Each of you should speak according to what you find pleasing.”
In the assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Dharmeśvara who said:
"O virtuous ones!
Arising and ceasing constitute duality."
“Phenomena are fundamentally unborn and are now without cessation; to attain this patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena is to enter the gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Virtue-Abiding said:
“‘Self’ and ‘what belongs to self’ constitute duality.”
"Because there is a self, there is 'what belongs to a self' (ātmīya);
if there were no self, there would be nothing that belongs to a self. This is what is meant by entering the gate of non-dual dharmas.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Animiṣa.
"To accept and not to accept constitute duality.
If a phenomenon is not accepted, it cannot be apprehended;
because it cannot be apprehended, there is neither grasping nor rejecting, neither action nor activity—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭa said:
"Defilement and purity are two.
To see the true nature of defilement, there is no mark of purity; to accord with the mark of cessation is to enter the gate of the non-dual Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Sunakṣatra said:
"This movement and this thought constitute duality.
Where there is no movement, there is no thought; where there is no thought, there is no discrimination. To penetrate this is to enter the gateway of the non-dual Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Sunetra said:
"The single characteristic and the absence of characteristics constitute two.

If one knows that the single characteristic is itself the absence of characteristics, and does not even grasp at the absence of characteristics, entering thereby into equanimity—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Subāhu said:
"The mind of a bodhisattva and the mind of a śrāvaka constitute duality.

To contemplate that the characteristics of the mind are empty and like an illusion or a magical transformation—such that there is neither a bodhisattva-mind nor a śrāvaka-mind—is to enter the gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Puṣya said:
"Good and not-good constitute duality.
If one does not give rise to good or not-good, but enters the limit of signlessness and attains thorough penetration, this is called entering the gate of non-dual dharmas."
The Bodhisattva Siṃha said:
"Sin and merit are two.

If one penetrates the nature of sin, it is no different from merit. To resolve this characteristic through adamantine wisdom, such that there is neither bondage nor liberation—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Siṃhamati said:
"The tainted and the untainted constitute duality.

If one realizes the equality of all phenomena, then the notions of 'tainted' and 'untainted' do not arise; one does not cling to signs, nor does one dwell in signlessness. This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhivimukti said:
"Conditioned and unconditioned constitute duality.
If one is free from all numerical designations, then the mind is like empty space; to be unimpeded through pure wisdom in this way is the entrance into the gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa said:
"The mundane and the supramundane constitute a duality.

The very nature of the mundane is empty; this is itself the supramundane. To neither enter nor exit it, neither to overflow nor to disperse within it—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Subhāṣita said:
"Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa constitute a duality.

If one perceives the nature of birth-and-death, then there is no birth-and-death; there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither arising nor ceasing. To understand it in this way is to enter the gate of non-dual dharmas."
The Bodhisattva Pratyakṣadarśin said:
"Exhaustion and non-exhaustion constitute duality.
Whether a phenomenon is ultimately exhausted or not exhausted, it possesses the characteristic of being inexhaustible."
The characteristic of inexhaustibility is itself emptiness; in emptiness, there is neither the characteristic of exhaustion nor the characteristic of non-exhaustion.
To enter in this manner is to enter the gateway of the non-dual Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Samantarakṣa said:
"Self and non-self constitute a duality.
Since even 'self' cannot be apprehended, how could 'non-self' be apprehended?"
"One who perceives my true nature no longer gives rise to duality; this is what is meant by entering the gate of non-dual dharmas.
The Bodhisattva Vidyuddeva said:
"Luminosity and ignorance constitute a duality."

The true nature of ignorance is itself clarity; yet this clarity is also ungraspable. It transcends all numerical categories; that which is equanimous and non-dual within it is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said:
"Form and the emptiness of form constitute two.
Form itself is emptiness; it is not that form ceases to exist for there to be emptiness, but rather the very nature of form is itself empty."

In this way, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and the emptiness of consciousness, constitute a duality. Consciousness itself is emptiness; it is not that consciousness ceases to be empty. The nature of consciousness is inherently empty. To penetrate this thoroughly is to enter the gateway of the non-dual Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhāsa said:
“The four elements are one thing and the element of emptiness is another; these two are distinct.
However, the nature of the four elements is itself the nature of the element of emptiness, because just as the past limit and the future limit are empty, so too is the middle limit empty.”
"If one can know all such natures in this way, this is called entering the gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Subtle Intention said:
"The eye and forms constitute duality.
If one knows the nature of the eye, one is without greed, hatred, or delusion regarding forms; this is called tranquility.

Likewise, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena constitute a duality. If one knows the nature of the mind, one is without greed, hatred, or delusion regarding mental phenomena; this is called tranquility. To abide within this is to enter the gate of the non-dual Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said:
“Giving and dedicating it toward omniscience constitute two.

The nature of giving is itself the nature of dedication toward omniscience. Likewise, observing the precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and dedicating them toward omniscience constitute two; the nature of wisdom is itself the nature of dedication toward omniscience. To enter into the single characteristic within this is to enter the gateway of non-dual dharmas.”
The Bodhisattva Gambhīramati said:
"To regard 'emptiness' and 'signlessness' as two is dualistic.
Emptiness is itself signlessness, and signlessness is itself non-action."

If emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are such that there is no mind, thought, or consciousness, and if these three gates of liberation are one and the same gate of liberation, this is the entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Śāntendriya said:
"Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha constitute duality.
The Buddha is the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Saṃgha; these Three Jewels all possess the characteristic of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and are equal to space; all dharmas are likewise so."
"One who can practice in accordance with this enters the gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Unobstructed Mind said:
"The body and the extinction of the body constitute a duality."
The body is itself the cessation of the body.

Why is this? One who perceives the true reality of the body does not give rise to the view of a body nor the view of its cessation; for the body and the cessation of the body are non-dual and without distinction. To be neither startled nor afraid within this is to enter the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Shangshan said:
"The actions of body, speech, and mind constitute duality.

These three types of action are all without the characteristic of activity; that which is without the characteristic of activity in the body is likewise without the characteristic of activity in speech."
The mark of non-action in speech is itself the mark of non-action in thought;
these three marks of non-action in the karmas of body, speech, and mind are themselves the mark of non-action in all phenomena.
One who can thus accord with the wisdom of non-action enters the gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Puṇyakṣetra said:
“Meritorious action, non-meritorious action, and immovable action constitute duality.
The true nature of these three types of action is emptiness; since they are empty, there is no meritorious action, no non-meritorious action, and no immovable action.”
"Not giving rise to these three modes of activity is what constitutes entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Flower Adornment said:
"To give rise to duality from the self is duality."
One who perceives the true reality of me does not give rise to dualistic dharmas;
if one does not abide in dualistic dharmas, then there is no consciousness.
To have nothing that is cognized is what constitutes entry into the gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Guṇasaṃbhava said:
“To have the mark of something obtainable is duality.
If there is nothing obtainable, then there is neither grasping nor rejecting.”
"To have neither grasping nor rejecting is to enter the gate of the non-dual Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Candrottara said,
"Darkness and light constitute a duality."
Where there is neither darkness nor light, there is no duality.

Why is this? Just as when one enters the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*), there is neither darkness nor light, so too it is with the characteristics of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-lakṣaṇa*). To enter into equality within this is what constitutes entering the gateway of non-dual dharmas (*advayadharmamukha*).
The Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta said:
“To delight in nirvāṇa and not to delight in the world constitutes duality.
If one neither delights in nirvāṇa nor feels aversion toward the world, then there is no duality.”
Why is this so? If there were bondage, then there would be liberation;
but if there has been no bondage from the very beginning, who is it that seeks liberation?
To be neither bound nor liberated is to be without joy or aversion; this is what is called entering the gate of non-dual dharmas.
Bodhisattva Maṇicūḍarāja said:
“The right path and the wrong path constitute duality.
"One who abides in the right path does not discriminate between what is wrong and what is right; to be free from these two is to enter the gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Ratisatya said:
"Reality and unreality constitute a duality.
Even one who perceives reality does not perceive reality; how much less so one who perceives what is unreal? Why is this?

It is not that which is seen by the physical eye, but rather that which the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) can see. Yet this wisdom-eye neither sees nor does not see; this is called entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
When each of these bodhisattvas had thus spoken, they asked Mañjuśrī,
"What is the bodhisattva’s entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality?
Mañjuśrī replied:

"In my view, regarding all phenomena, there is no speech and no discourse, no demonstration and no cognition; being free from all questioning and answering—this is what it means to enter the gateway of non-duality."
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti: "We have each spoken for ourselves;
now, virtuous one, you should explain what constitutes the bodhisattva’s entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality."
At that time, Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word.
Mañjuśrī praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"Even to the point where there are no words or speech—this is the true entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.

When this "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality" was being spoken, five thousand bodhisattvas within this assembly all entered the Dharma-gate of non-duality and attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Chapter Ten: The Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation.
At that time, Śāriputra thought to himself:
"The time for the midday meal is approaching; where shall these bodhisattvas eat?"
Then Vimalakīrti, knowing his thoughts, said to him:
"The Buddha has taught the eight liberations; you, O worthy one, have accepted and practiced them. How can you listen to the Dharma while your mind is distracted by the desire for food?"
"If you wish to eat, wait but a moment; I shall cause you to obtain food such as you have never experienced before.

At that time, Vimalakīrti entered into samādhi and, by means of his supernormal powers, revealed to the great assembly the region above, beyond Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers. There was a land named Saugandhika, where the Buddha was named Gandhottama, who currently resides there.
The fragrance of that land surpasses the scents of humans and devas in all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions; it is the most supreme of all.
In that land, there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; there are only assemblies of pure great bodhisattvas, for whom the Buddha preaches the Dharma.
In that realm, everything consists of pavilions made of fragrance; there are fragrant grounds for walking meditation, and the gardens and groves are all fragrant.
The scent of its food circulates throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions.

At that time, while that Buddha was sitting together with the bodhisattvas to partake of a meal, there were sons of gods all named Gandhavimāna who had all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They made offerings to that Buddha and the bodhisattvas, and there was no one among this great assembly who did not witness it with their own eyes.
Then Vimalakīrti asked the assembly of bodhisattvas:
"Virtuous ones! Who among you is able to bring back the food of that Buddha?"
Because of Mañjuśrī’s majestic spiritual power, everyone remained silent.
Vimalakīrti said,
"O virtuous ones, is this great assembly not to be put to shame?"
Mañjuśrī said, "As the Buddha has spoken, do not disparage those who have not yet studied.

Thereupon, Vimalakīrti, without rising from his seat, manifested before the assembly a bodhisattva— endowed with the marks and signs of excellence, radiant, and of such sublime majesty that he outshone the entire gathering— and addressed him, saying:

“Go to the region above; past as many Buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Saṃghagandha, where the Buddha is named Gandhottama, who is currently sitting together with various bodhisattvas to partake of a meal.”
