without fear and without sorrow, without joy, without weariness, and without attachment.
It has not existed in the past, it will not exist in the future, and it does not exist in the present;
it cannot be displayed through any verbal expression or conceptual discrimination.
World-Honored One!
The body of the Tathāgata is such as this; one who contemplates it in this manner is said to have right contemplation;
if one contemplates it otherwise, it is called wrong contemplation.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Vimalakīrti,
"From where did you pass away to come and be born here?
Vimalakīrti replied:
“Is there any passing away or birth in the Dharma you have attained?
Śāriputra replied,
“There is neither passing away nor birth.”
"If all phenomena have no characteristic of passing away or being born, why do you ask:
'From where did you pass away to come and be born here?
What do you think?"
“Suppose, for example, there were a magician who conjured up men and women by illusion;
would they die or be born? Śāriputra replied, “They neither die nor are they born.”
“Have you not heard the Buddha teach that all dharmas have the characteristic of being like an illusion? He replied, “It is so!”
"If all phenomena have the characteristic of being like an illusion, why do you ask:
'From where did you pass away to come and be born here? Śāriputra!"
That which perishes is a dharma of falsehood, characterized by decay;
that which arises is a dharma of falsehood, characterized by continuity.
Although a bodhisattva passes away, they do not exhaust their roots of goodness.
"Although they are born there, they do not increase their various evils.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"There is a land named Abhirati, and the Buddha there is named Akṣobhya."
"This Vimalakīrti has passed away from that land and come to be born here.
Śāriputra said, "This is truly unprecedented!"
“World-Honored One!
This person is truly able to abandon a pure land and come to delight in this place of much anger and harm.
Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra:
"What do you think?
When the sun rises, does it join with the darkness?
He replied:
"No! When the sun rises, all darkness immediately vanishes.
Vimalakīrti said:
"Why does the sun travel over Jambudvīpa?
He replied,
"It is because it desires to illuminate and thereby dispel the darkness."
Vimalakīrti said:
“It is thus with the bodhisattva!

Although he is born in impure buddha-fields, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he does not conjoin with ignorance and darkness; rather, he merely extinguishes the darkness of the afflictions of sentient beings!”
At that time, the great assembly was filled with longing, desiring to behold the world of Abhirati, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and his host of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Knowing the thoughts of the entire gathering, the Buddha addressed Vimalakīrti, saying:
"O son of good family!
"For the sake of this assembly, I wish for everyone to behold the Land of Wonderful Joy, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and the multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti thought to himself:

“Without rising from my seat, I shall receive the Iron Ring Mountains, rivers, streams, valleys, great oceans, springs, Mount Sumeru, and all the mountains, as well as the sun, moon, and stars; the palaces of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and brahmās; along with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas; the cities, towns, villages, men and women, both great and small, up to the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Bodhi tree, and the various exquisite lotuses that perform the Buddha-work throughout the ten directions—the Triple-Path Jewel Staircase leading from Jambudvīpa to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, by which staircases the devas descend to pay homage to the Tathāgata Akṣobhya and listen to the Dharma.
The people of Jambudvīpa shall likewise ascend these stairs to rise to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and behold those devas.”

The world-system Abhirati has thus accomplished such immeasurable merits—from the Akaniṣṭha Heaven above down to the water’s edge below—that [the Buddha] takes it up with his right hand like a potter’s wheel and brings it into this world, as if holding a garland of flowers, to show it to all the assemblies.
Having formed this thought, he entered into samādhi and manifested supernormal powers, using his right hand to cut off and take up the world-system of Abhirati, placing it within this land.
The Bodhisattvas who had attained supernatural powers, the assembly of Śrāvakas, and the other devas and humans all raised their voices together, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
Who has taken us away? We pray that you will rescue and protect us.”
The Buddha Akṣobhya said, "This was not done by me;
it was performed through the supernatural power of Vimalakīrti.
Those others who had not yet attained supernormal powers were neither aware of nor knew where they themselves had gone."
Although the world of Abhirati enters this land, it neither increases nor decreases; likewise, this world is not constricted, remaining no different than before.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"Behold now the world of Abhirati, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the adornments of his land, the purity of the bodhisattvas' conduct, and the stainlessness of his disciples."
They all replied,
“Indeed, we have seen them.
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva wishes to attain such a pure buddha-field, they should study the path practiced by the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.

When this Land of Wonderful Joy was manifested, fourteen nayutas of people from the Sahā world resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all vowing to be born in the buddha-field of Wonderful Joy.
Śākyamuni Buddha then gave him this prediction:
"You shall be born in that land.
At that time, after the world of Abhirati had finished performing all the deeds necessary for the benefit of this realm, it returned to its original place, and the entire assembly witnessed this.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
“Do you see this world of Abhirati and the Buddha Akṣobhya?
“Indeed, I see them, World-Honored One!”
May all sentient beings attain a pure land like that of the Buddha Akṣobhya,
and obtain supernormal powers like those of Vimalakīrti.
World-Honored One!
We have gained a great and wholesome benefit in being able to see this person and to draw near to him and make offerings to him.
Furthermore, those sentient beings who, whether in the present or after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, hear this sutra, will also gain a wholesome benefit;
how much more so for those who, having heard it, believe and understand it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain it, and practice according to the Dharma?
If there are those who obtain this sutra with their hands, they have already obtained the treasury of the Dharma-jewel;
if there are those who read, recite, explain its meaning, and practice according to the teaching, they shall be protected and remembered by all Buddhas;
and if there are those who make offerings to such persons, you should know that they are making offerings to the Buddha himself.
Wherever there is one who writes down or upholds this sutra scroll, know that the Tathāgata is present in that very room;
if anyone hears this sutra and can rejoice in it, such a person has already attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*);

and if anyone can believe and understand even a single four-line verse of this sutra and explain it to others, know that this person has received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
13. Chapter on the Dharma-Reliquary Offering. In the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, Chapter Thirteen: At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, amidst the great assembly, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Although I have heard hundreds of thousands of sūtras from the Buddha and Mañjuśrī, I have never before heard this inconceivable sūtra of sovereign supernormal powers and definitive reality.

As I understand the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has taught, if there are sentient beings who hear this sutra-dharma and believe, understand, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, they will certainly attain this dharma without doubt; how much more so for those who practice according to the teaching?
Such a person shall close the gates to all evil destinies and open the doors to all wholesome paths; they will be constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas;
they shall subdue those of external teachings and crush the enmity of Māra;
they shall cultivate and refine bodhi and dwell securely at the site of enlightenment.
I shall tread upon the tracks traversed by the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!
If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice according to the teaching, I shall, together with my retinue, provide offerings and attend to their needs.
In whatever villages, towns, cities, mountain forests, or wildernesses this sutra may be found, I too shall go to those places together with my retinue in order to hear and receive the Dharma;
those who have not yet developed faith, I shall cause to develop faith, and those who already have faith, I shall provide protection for.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent,
O Lord of Devas!”
As you have said, I rejoice in your words.
This sutra extensively explains the inconceivable *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Therefore, O Lord of Devas!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, recites, and makes offerings to this sutra, they are thereby making offerings to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
"O Lord of Devas!
Suppose the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were filled with Tathāgatas, as densely as a grove of sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, rice, hemp, or forest thickets.

If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for one kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, honored, revered, praised, and made offerings to them, providing all that they required; and after the parinirvāṇa of those Buddhas, erected for each of their entire bodily relics a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels—extending in length and breadth over one four-continent world-system and rising as high as the Brahma-heaven, adorned with a pinnacle and banner—and for one kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, made offerings to them with every kind of flower, incense, necklace, banner, flag, and the most exquisite and supreme music; what do you think, O Lord of Devas? Would the merit planted by such a person not be vast?"
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
“It is much,
World-Honored One!”
"The merit of that person could not be fully exhausted even if it were explained for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas.
The Buddha told Śakra:

"You should know that if a son or daughter of good family hears this *Sūtra of the Inconceivable Liberation*, believes, understands, upholds, recites, and practices it, their merit will be far greater than that."
Why is this so? Because the bodhi of all Buddhas arises from this;
the characteristics of bodhi are immeasurable, and for this reason, the merit is also immeasurable.
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:

"In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in that world named Bhaiṣajyarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
The world was named Great Adornment, the eon was called Adornment, and the Buddha’s lifespan was twenty minor eons.
His assembly of śrāvakas numbered thirty-six billion nayutas, and his assembly of bodhisattvas numbered one billion two hundred million.
"O Lord of Devas!
At that time, there was a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Ratnacchattra, who possessed the seven treasures and ruled over the four continents.
The king had a thousand sons, all handsome, brave, and strong, capable of subduing enemies."
"At that time, Ratnacchattra and his retinue made offerings to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, providing all necessities for his comfort for a full five kalpas.
After these five kalpas had passed, he addressed his thousand sons:
'You also should, like me, make offerings to the Buddha with a profound mind.'"
Thereupon, the thousand sons received their father the king’s command and made offerings to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja for another five kalpas, providing all manner of comforts and security.
Among them, one son named Candracchattra sat alone in contemplation, thinking:
"Is there perhaps a way to make an offering even more extraordinary than this?"
By the supernatural power of the Buddha, a deva in the air said:
"Good son! The offering of the Dharma surpasses all other offerings."
He then asked:
"What is meant by the 'Dharma-offering'?
The deva replied:
“You should go and inquire of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja; he shall extensively explain for you the offering of the Dharma.
Thereupon, Prince Candracchattra went to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme.
What constitutes the offering of the Dharma?
The Buddha said:

"Good son! As for the Dharma-offering, it consists of the profound sūtras spoken by all Buddhas, which are difficult for all the world to believe and accept, subtle and difficult to perceive, pure and untainted, and not something that can be attained through mere conceptual discrimination or thought. It is encompassed within the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas, sealed with the seal of dhāraṇīs;
it leads to the stage of non-retrogression, accomplishes the six perfections, skillfully distinguishes meanings, accords with the Dharma of Bodhi, and stands at the pinnacle of all sūtras."
Entering into great compassion, they remain free from all demonic activities and false views;
they accord with the law of dependent origination, realizing there is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span; they abide in emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-arising;
they are able to cause sentient beings to sit at the site of enlightenment and turn the wheel of Dharma, receiving the praise and acclaim of devas, nāgas, gandharvas, and others.
They enable sentient beings to enter the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, encompassing all the wisdom of the worthy and holy ones;
they expound the path practiced by all bodhisattvas;
and relying on the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, they clearly proclaim the teachings of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and cessation.
It is able to rescue all sentient beings who violate the precepts; it can cause fear in all demons, non-Buddhists, and those who are greedily attached; it is praised by all Buddhas and worthy sages;
it turns one’s back on the suffering of birth and death and reveals the bliss of nirvana; it is what has been taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

If one hears such sutras as these, and with faith and understanding accepts, maintains, reads, and recites them, and uses the power of skillful means to analyze, explain, and clearly demonstrate them for the sake of all sentient beings in order to protect the Dharma—this is called the "Dharma-offering."

Furthermore, they practice all dharmas according to the teachings, accord with the twelve links of dependent origination, and, free from all false views, attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
They are certain that there is no self and no sentient beings, yet they neither oppose nor dispute the fruits of causes and conditions; they are free from the notion of "mine.

They rely on the meaning and not on the words, rely on wisdom and not on consciousness, rely on sūtras of definitive meaning and not on sūtras of provisional meaning, and rely on the Dharma and not on persons.
Conforming to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), there is nothing entered and nothing returned to;

because ignorance is ultimately extinguished, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are also ultimately extinguished, and so on, until because birth is ultimately extinguished, old age and death are also ultimately extinguished.

To contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in this way—without perceiving any sign of exhaustion and no longer giving rise to views—is called the supreme offering of the Dharma.
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:
“Prince Candracchattra, having heard this Dharma from the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja, attained the patience of compliance (anulomikī-kṣānti).
He immediately removed his precious robes and bodily ornaments to offer them as a gift to the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:”
“World-Honored One!
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, I shall practice the offering of the Dharma and protect the True Dharma.
I pray that you will empower me with your majestic spiritual power and compassion to establish me, so that I may subdue the enmity of Māra and cultivate the bodhisattva practices.”
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in his deep mind, prophesied to him, saying:
"In the final age, you shall guard the city of the Dharma. O Devendra!
At that time, Prince Candracchattra, having seen the purity of the Dharma and heard the Buddha’s prophecy, left the household life out of faith and cultivated wholesome dharmas.
Before long, through diligent effort, he attained the five supernormal powers, reached the bodhisattva path, and acquired dhāraṇīs and uninterrupted eloquence.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, by means of the power of the supernormal knowledges, dhāraṇīs, and eloquence he had attained, for ten intermediate kalpas he shall propagate throughout all directions the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja.

The bhikṣu Candracchattra, through his diligent practice of vigor for the sake of guarding the Dharma, established one hundred trillion people in this very life in the state of non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
fourteen *nayuta* of people deeply resolved their minds toward the paths of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha;
and immeasurable sentient beings attained rebirth in the heavens.
"O Lord of Devas!
Was King Ratnacchattra anyone else at that time?
He is none other than the one who has now attained Buddhahood, known as the Tathāgata Ratnārcis."
The king’s thousand sons are none other than the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa—beginning with K Krakucchanda as the first to attain Buddhahood and ending with the Tathāgata named Ruci.
The bhikṣu Candracchattra was none other than myself.
Thus, O Śakra, Lord of Devas,
you should know this essential point:
The offering of the Dharma is the highest among all offerings, the most supreme, the foremost,
and peerless. Therefore, O Devendra,
you should honor the Buddha with the offering of the Dharma.
14. Chapter on the Entrustment. In the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Chapter Fourteen, the Entrustment, the Buddha then addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: “Maitreya!
I now entrust to you this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which I have accumulated over immeasurable billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Such sutras as these, during the final age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you must use your supernormal powers to propagate widely throughout Jambudvīpa, ensuring that they do not come to an end.

Why is this? In future ages, there will be good men and good women, as well as devas, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and others, who will resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and delight in the Great Dharma;
if they do not hear sūtras such as these, they will lose their opportunity for wholesome benefit.

When people of such caliber hear sūtras of this kind, they will surely have much faith and joy, give rise to a sense of rare wonder, and receive them upon the crown of their heads; they shall then expound them extensively according to the benefits that should be gained by all sentient beings.
“Maitreya! You should know that there are two characteristics of a bodhisattva. What are these two?
First, they take pleasure in miscellaneous phrases and ornamental rhetoric;
second, they do not fear profound meanings and are able to enter them as they truly are.
If one takes pleasure in miscellaneous phrases and ornamental rhetoric, it should be known that this is a newly initiated bodhisattva.

If one has no fear regarding such profound sūtras that are untainted and unattached, and is able to enter into them; having heard them, one’s mind becomes pure, and one receives, maintains, recites, and practices according to the teaching—know that this person has long cultivated the path of practice.
“Maitreya! Furthermore, there are two qualities that characterize a novice who is unable to reach a definitive understanding of the profound Dharma.
What are these two?
First, upon hearing profound sutras never heard before, they are struck with alarm and fear, giving rise to doubt; unable to accord with them, they slander and do not believe them, saying:
"I have never heard these before; from where have they come?"

Second, if there are those who protect, uphold, and explain such profound sutras, one is unwilling to draw near to them, make offerings to them, or show them respect; or at times, one speaks of their faults and evils.
If these two dharmas are present, you should know that this is a newly initiated bodhisattva who brings about self-injury and is unable to discipline his mind within the profound Dharma.

“Maitreya! Furthermore, there are two dharmas by which a bodhisattva, despite having faith and understanding in the profound dharma, still brings about self-injury and is unable to attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).”
What are these two?
First, to treat newly initiated bodhisattvas with contempt and fail to instruct them;
second, although one understands the profound Dharma, to grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination.
"These are the two dharmas.
Having heard this teaching, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
It is truly unprecedented!
As the Buddha has taught, I shall distance myself from such evils and uphold the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which the Tathāgata has accumulated over countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

If there are good men or good women in future ages who seek the Mahāyāna, you should cause them to obtain such sūtras as these in their hands, bestow upon them the power of mindfulness, and enable them to receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively expound them for others.
World-Honored One!
If, in the future final age, there are those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it to others, you should know that these are all established through the spiritual power of Maitreya.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Maitreya!"
“As you have said, the Buddha rejoices in your joy.
Then all the bodhisattvas joined their palms and addressed the Buddha:

“We, too, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, shall widely proclaim and disseminate the Dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the lands of the ten directions; furthermore, we shall instruct and guide those who preach the Dharma, so that they may obtain this sutra.”
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

In whatever places—whether cities, towns, villages, mountain forests, or wilderness—there may be this scripture, and those who read, recite, explain, or expound it, we shall lead our respective retinues to go to those locations for the sake of hearing the Dharma. We will protect those individuals within a radius of one hundred yojanas, ensuring that no one seeking an opportunity to harm them can find an opening."
At that time, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Receive and uphold this sutra, and propagate it widely.
Ānanda said:
“Yes, indeed!
I have already received and upheld the essentials,
World-Honored One.”
"What should this sutra be named?
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
This sutra is titled "The Teaching of Vimalakīrti," and it is also titled "The Dharma Gate of Inconceivable Liberation"; thus should it be upheld.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the elder Vimalakīrti, Mañjuśrī, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the entire great assembly—including gods, humans, and asuras—having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all filled with great joy.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll II.
